THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Eddie Barefield
Cassette 1
November 20, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
When were you born?
December 12th, 1909.
Oh, we're both Sagittarians, I'm the 18th.
Oh, yes. I have about six people in my family who are Sagittarians. My brother, my sister and I, my brother, we're all born in December. And I have a grandson who was born on the same day I was born.
That's unusual. Now, your family came from where?
Well, my father was from Texas. He was born in Austin, Texas. My mother was born in Oklahoma. Muskogee.
There have been a few people from there who have gone on to play.
Right, right.
And were they musically inclined at all?

Well, my father was what you would call -- he wasn't a musician. He played the guitar and sang the blues and things like that. Of course, he was a coal miner and, you know, they used to sing after they got out of work. My mother played piano when I was little. She was taking piano lessons. But none of them became professional or even
made a hobby out of it.
Was there any music around you?

Well, we always had phonograph records, as far back as I can remember. Even back in the days when they made the cylinder records we had records. We used to listen to all of the music that was played at that time.
What was Scandia like?
I don't remember because --
You moved?

No, Scandia doesn't exist any more. Des Moines engulfed it. It was a coal town and like all the other coal towns, most of them in Iowa, are dried up now. And those that were close around the city of Des Moines were engulfed by the city. Most of the people moved to the suburbs and made these towns into a suburban area.
Now, how long did you stay there? Went to school there?
Yes, I went to grade school and high school in Des Moines. And I left Des Moines when I was about 16.
When did you start playing an instrument?
When I was 11. I started piano when I was 9.
And then -- it says here, alto sax at 13, is that about right?

Well, I started to play it -- I was playing professionally by then. But my mother got me an alto sax when I was 12. AND to start out. before and it took me about a year, in fact, I had played piano and a week after I got my first saxophone I played my first job the next week.
(Laughter)
How did that come about?

The story is that, if you want me to tell it from the beginning, my intention was to be a fighter. My father was a boxer. He was also a coal miner but he boxed around and he had taught me the pugilistic art. you know. And I was pretty good when I was a kid, when I was 5 or 6 years old. That was my intention because I used to buy all the literature on Jack Johnson, I had a whole scrapbook of him. And I was a Jack Dempsey fan. So I was going to be a fighter.

Across the street from me lived a fellow who was taking piano, he was about 11 and I was about 9 at the time. He wanted -- we were to be friends, his name was Merle Williams. M-e-r-l-e. He said to me, look, what do you want to be a fighter for? Why don't you play music. I said, you know, I never thought of that things. He said, well, come

on and study piano. He took me to his piano teacher, a lady named Josephine Guy, that's right. And I started studying piano and practicing on his piano because we didn't have a piano at home. I studied piano about a year and was doing pretty good. But the kids in the neighborhood started calling me a sissy because I was playing piano so I didn't want to play the piano, I gave it up. And one day Merle came over to my house and said, they're organizing a community band. And they're going to furnish the instruments so why don't you come along and get in the band. I said, 'well, all right, but what instrument should I play?' He said, 'well, a French horn is a beautiful instrument, why don't you play that?'

Well, to please him I went along with him. We went to this meeting and when we got there there was an old man and his name was Mr. Warwick (PHONETIC). He was playing a C melody saxophone. And I had never seen a saxophone before to notice it. And I said, what instrument is that? He said, 'that's a saxophone, C melody.' I said, 'well, that's the instrument I'd like to play.'

So I signed up for saxophone. Well, this orchestra never did materialize, we never did get the instruments or anything. But I had made up my mind that I wanted to be a saxophone player so I told my mother --
You just liked the look of it?

Yeah, I just liked the looks of it. I told my mother I wanted a saxophone. She said, 'well, I've spent money with you for piano lessons and you gave it up. Do you think you'll stick with this?' I said, 'Mama, get me a saxophone and I'll learn to play it.' And I wanted a C melody saxophone because, see, you didn't have to transpose, in those days. You could play from the piano sheet. So anyway, we were strong believers in Christmas and Santa Claus, you know. This Christmas, sure enough when I woke up Christmas morning, under the Christmas tree was a brand new York (PHONETIC) alto saxophone. And there was a note that said, 'Santa Claus didn't have any more C melodies but he said the alto is going to be very popular so this is the one you should learn.' All right, great. I took the instrument and now -- I was sort of mechanically inclined in those days and the first thing I did was take all the keys off to see how it was put together. And then my mother she was flabbergasted, you know. She had to put it all in a bag, keys and all, and take it back down to the store and have it reassembled. When she brought it back she said, 'Now, you can't touch it until I get you a teacher.' So she found me a teacher whose name was Charles Bushman, lived on 9th Street in Des Moines. And she took me to him; 50 cents a lesson. The first lesson, he taught me the

chromatic scale. Well, that's all I needed. I went home and we had records all of these years and I started fooling around playing what those little things I had in my ear. And I started copying Coleman Hawkins who was the first saxophone player that I remember hearing. And he was recording with Fletcher Henderson's band in 1923. I remember when they picked him up and brought him -- Fletcher Henderson and Mamie Smith brought him out of St. Joseph, Missouri.

I started to learn these things from the record. When my mother gave me the 50 cents every week to take the lesson, I would go deposit myself horn in the drug store and go to the movies and then come home and practice with the records. She would say, "is that your lesson?" And I would say, "fine", yes, that's my lesson." This is actually the way I learned how to play. I didn't know scales or chords about.
You were an ear player?
Yeah. So anyway --
Did you read any music at this time?

No, no. Well, I read from the -- I knew notes because I had studied piano. But I didn't apply it to saxophone. So Merle, we got together and we got a little group together. A friend of mine named LeRoy White used to come, his parents knew my parents, they lived in

Perry, Iowa. He used to come down and he was a trumpet player. And we got the three of us together and we got made a little band. And then we added another little drummer named Melvin Saunders and we had a four piece band which we called the Jim Gem Town Ramblers (PHONETIC). We started playing around together, and playing at school parties, and playing at kids' parties and everything.
You were about 13 at this time?

Yes. And so we started sounding pretty good so we started taking the adult jobs from the regular band there in town which was called the Joy Generators, George Ann Raiders. They were older fellows and they used to come and hear us play. And I remember distinctly how when we played how these guys would squinch their faces because I imagine it sounded pretty rough. But we got better and better and started playing their dances and things.

And after time went on, maybe we played together a couple of years, we used to rehearse every Sunday, and we would copy things from the records. But Roy, the trumpet player, his father was a trumpet teacher in Perry and he was the only one of us that could read besides Merle, the piano player. The drummer was playing by ear and I, but I would just follow along. Because previous to that when I was 6 or 7 years old, I sang in a school group, you know. We had a quartet and the teacher used to take us from place to place singing.
I had a pretty good ear for harmony.

Around 1925, I was downtown one day and they were building the Capital Theater on Grand Avenue. I had gone to the music store and bought an orchestration on "Aggravating Papa," I think it was. And as I was going home there was a hod carrier who came over to me you know, put his stick there and said, hey, son, what's that you've got? Music? I said, "yes." He said, "well, let me see it." I showed it to him and he said, "well, could I have a second trumpet part, do you have it? I said, "yes," because we didn't have but one trumpet. He said, "what are you going to do with this music?" I said, "well, we've got a little band and we're going to play." he said, "May I come and hear your band?" Yes.

His name was Edgar Pillows (PHONETIC) and he was an older man. He came up one day and he heard us rehearse. He got himself an E flat tuba and started rehearsing with us. He finally took us over and called us Edgar Pillows' Night Owls. It was just the five of us. No, we had one more man, older man, which was a banjo player, Emery Henry Green. So it was Edgar Pillows who was the leader, Emery Henry Green the banjo player and --
Trumpet and alto?
Trumpet and alto.
Piano and --
Piano and drums. We really started playing for homecomings around and playing all over the state, different places.
How much older was he?

Oh, Edgar -- we were kids, say the oldest of us was about 16 and he was in his 20's, you know. Emery and Edgar Henry Green was in his 30's or maybe near 40, he was a much older guy. But then Melvin Saunders the little fellow, the drummer, he was so young that we had to leave him off and we got an older drummer named Carl Shelton. He was a tap dancer and a drummer.

We played around the state there for quite a bit and played all the dances and things, after school, of course, and on weekends. In 1926 Edgar got a job playing for Miss Nebraska. Every year at that time -- I don't know if they still have it, they have an international beauty contest in Galveston, Texas. And all of the beauty queens of each state, they'd go there to compete. Well, Miss Nebraska, her entourage or whatever, hired us through Edgar Pillows to play on her train from Omaha to New Orleans and back. They set up a whole coach like a dancehall. And we played on this coach and we stopped over in different places. We stopped in a place called Hot Springs, Arkansas and Little Rock and Smack Over, Arkansas, which is an oil town. And we ended up
in New Orleans, we stayed there about a week or so. Then we went to Galveston, Texas.

And in Galveston I met Alphonso Trent (PHONETIC) who was one of the outstanding bands out there. In fact, one of the guys that was with him is here in New York now, Leo Mosley, Snub Mosley (PHONETIC). Well, he was in that band at that time. And we stayed around there about 10 days in Galveston and then we came back to Des Moines. You know, back to Omaha and back to Des Moines. But we played on this train, only on the train, for her for Miss Nebraska and her party.

Then when we got back to Des Moines we had the fever so we'd sit there saying, let's get something else. So we finally got a job on a carnival. And it was a little, dinky carnival, I don't remember the name of it. But we traveled by trucks, you know. So we were in this carnival and slept in the tent, and all of this thing.

So we were playing and we went to Madison, Wisconsin Madison, Iowa. And I remember when we left Madison, we had to sleep in the boxcar with all of the equipment and things going to the next town which was Atuma, Iowa. Well, when we got into Atuma, we played a week then we went to Iowa City.

And in Iowa City, a fellow There was they had another carnival which was playing in the next town from us called Isler Greater Shows, I-s-l-e-r, Greater, G-r-e-a-t-e-r Shows. Most people get that wrong. They call it the Gravy Show, but it's Greater.

The and this fellow that ran the Minstrel Show was named Rasus Jones (PROMOTER). and He heard us and he came over and said, well, "I'd like to get three of you, the trumpet player and the saxophone, you, Eddie, and the piano player to come over and join our Minstrel Show." Well, we were kids; we didn't know how to go about it. So in the middle of the night we sneaked off from the show and went over to the other. We were getting $10.00 a week in this first show. Well, He gave us $15.00 a week and a stateroom on the train. They had a whole train like a circus, you know, and they gave each one of us a room on the train where we could live and $15.00 a week. So this was quite a thing.

Well, we traveled all through Iowa and then we went down into Kansas, and we went to -- in fact, when we were in Leavenworth, Kansas I met George Lee who was a band out of orchestra and Kansas City and he was with his sister, Julia Lee. And I went out that night and set in with them. Then I met a fellow in the Army whose name was Sawyer. And He wanted me to join the Army Sawyer was a saxophone player in the Army band. And, you know, I was a jazz man. I didn't know how to play anything else.
Had you learned to read by this time?

Not yet. Because everything I played was just off the top of my head. I didn't know anything about harmony or chords or anything. But everywhere I played everybody thought I was a great jazz man. In those days, you know,

jazz hadn't developed really gotten to the place where it is today. So every town I went to -- every chance I had to play extra, go out and jam or something, I did. Sawyer wanted me to join the Army out there and get in the Army band. It was a three year stretch and I said, no, I didn't want to get hung up. I stayed with the carnival, we traveled all down through Kansas and Arkansas and Texas. That year is the year I went to San Antonio and I met Herschel Evans. He was a kid.
Yeah, playing with a local band?

Yeah, he was just beginning to learn to play then, too. We finished and finally we ended up in Pittsburgh, Kansas, around about two or three days before Labor Day, or the day before Labor Day. Now, I had promised my mother that if she would let me go on this carnival or go with Edgar Pillows out on the road that I would come back and go to school in September. It was getting close and I didn't want to go back home and go back to school.

We decided to leave the carnival and go to Kansas City, Merle and -- we had a drummer with us named Pete Washington on this show. And he lived around Kansas City so we all decided to go to Kansas City. But we still didn't know how to leave so we decided to run off in the middle of the night. We found out the train time out of Pitts-

burgh. So I had -- my mother, before I left, had left Des Moines, I had a new Buscher (PHONETIC) alto with -- silver alto with gold keys and everything. So I didn't have any money by the time we got ready to leave so I pawned the alto in Pittsburgh, Kansas for $40.00, which is still there.
Mr. It's still there?
(Laughter.)
Mr. Barefield: As far as I know.
So Merle and Roy and Pete and myself, we said, well, we'll meet at the railroad station about train time to go to Kansas City. This was the morning of Labor Day.

1926. So that morning we all were there. Everybody got to the station but Roy, the trumpet player. And the train came and we got on the train and he got left. So we went on in to Kansas City and I don't have any instrument. But anyway, that day was Labor Day and everything was happening there. They had dances there, George Lee was playing one place, Bennie Moten was playing someplace else. So I made all the dances because I wanted to hear the bands. This is the first time I'd met Lamar Wright who later came with Cab Calloway. He was playing with Bennie Moten at that time.

So I was there without an instrument so I'd had to try to find my way to make some kind of -- I didn't want to let my mother know I was there because I knew she would send for me. So I bummed around Kansas City for two or three days, living
slept in the park and slept in the post office at night.
What were the other guys doing?
Oh, well, Roy didn't -- Merle finally went on back to Des Moines. And Pete, he disappeared from the scene.
So you were there by yourself?

I'm there by myself. So I finally run into, after sleeping in the post office here and slept in LaSalle Park (PHONETIC) a couple nights and it was getting kind of cool. I ran into a fellow that I used to box with when I was selling newspapers in Des Moines. All this time I belonged to the newsboys and the Y and I used to box on Wednesday night for Tommy Ryan who had the Des Moines ATHLETIC Club there, we'd fight preliminaries. And I run into this guy, his name was Eddie Hilliard, he was washing dishes down by the post office there on Independence Avenue in Kansas City. And he said, well, I'll let you work one night, wash dishes one night, and I'll was dishes the next night. And we alternated like that, that's where I made myself a couple dollars, you know, and I got me a room.

So one day I was walking up by Lincoln Hall on 18th and Vine and I heard music. So I go upstairs and there was a bunch of kids up there playing. And there was a bunch of fellows from Pittsburgh, they were on their way to California, Raymond --
Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania?

Yeah, Raymond Valentine, who they called Sid Valentine, turned out to be a marvelous trumpet player. I'll tell you about him later because we played together later. And a few other fellows, I don't remember who it was. But anyway, I asked them to let me play -- their saxophone player, can I play your horn? So I sat in and played and they fell in love with me right away. So they said, what are you doing here? And I said, well, I'm just in Kansas City. "Well, you want to go to California?" "Fine, I'd like to go," I said, "but I don't have a horn." They said, don't worry, we'll get you a horn.

Well, the next week they were supposed to leave and I was home in my room and that morning I heard the doorbell ring and somebody said, "you have a boy here named Ed Barefield?" And I heard the lady say yes, and a friend of my mother's walked in. She had sent him to bring me home. So I didn't get a chance to contact these fellows again. So I just went on home with him, home to my mother. And she made me go back to school.

But I wasn't happy, I wanted to play. I didn't have a horn, so I borrowed a C melody saxophone from a friend of mine and I played around Des Moines all that winter with this horn. And there was a friend of mine from Chicago who lived in Des Moines and he was home visiting. Came home Christmas

to visit his family, named Bill Fulton. And he wanted me to teach him how to play jazz on the saxophone. So I was giving him lessons, teaching him the way I played. And he said, what are you doing staying around Des Moines for? You should be in Chicago, he says, "much as you play," you know. Of course, the only thing that reading hadn't come in our minds, so we were saying interested -- we were interested, just playing -- improvising.
Yet by this time there were, you know, the big bands.
Not yet. Oh, that's in New York. But the biggest thing we had out there was one time a band came there called the Midnight Ramblers, had about eight pieces.
What about McKinney's Cotton Pickers?
They hadn't started yet, either. Cotton Pickers didn't come out until about 1928, you know, like that.
So most of the bands were --
Most of the bands were small bands --
(Inaudible) had arrangements?

They had quite a few big white bands that used to play at the Cotillion Ballroom. We'd climb up and listen to them play. I don't remember all their names. But most of the bands were eight, seven, six -- in fact, all up through the late twenties the big band was a ten piece band.
You know, up until say 1930. You had a ten piece band, you had two trumpets and two altos and a tenor and four rhythm, that was a big band.

Anyway, Bill said, 'why don't you go to Chicago?' I said, 'well, man, I don't know how to' -- he said, 'Good as you play, you should be in Chicago.' So we decided that when he went back to Chicago I would go. So I didn't have money, you know, to go like that. Of course, I wanted to go for the very simple reason my mother wouldn't let me work. She wanted me to go to school and I wanted to work and help her support my brother and sister because my father had died when I was 11, in 1921.

But she wouldn't have it. She wanted me to -- in fact, I got a job one time working during this time I was back, I got a job working with the cement plant. And I worked a week and she finally looked at my eyes at suppertime and saw the cement in my eyes. And she said, have you been going to school? And I had to confess. Well, she made me go back to school.
So anyway, in the spring when Bill got ready to go back to Chicago we had set up a deal that he would take my instrument on the train and I was going to hobo to Chicago, which all of the --
You still had the C melody?
NO, I had an alto by now. I had gotten an alto and it was a York alto, another York alto.

Because I had to return this fellow's C melody. So I made it up -- of course, a lot of the older boys, Albert Snyder who was older than me, they used to do it for a lark, just get on a train, hobo to Chicago, hang around there for a few days and come back. So I got contact with him because I had never done it before. So he said, 'well, I'll go with you,' Albert Snyder said he'd go with me. So we had it all set up so that we would let Bill take the horn on the train and we'd both catch that same train that night and go to Chicago.

Well, that day -- I used to divide my time with my grandmother who lived on the east side and my mother who lived on the west side. So this day I told my grandmother that I would stay with my mother that night and I got up and put on my suit, which was a common thing, put my overalls over my suit, and I went onto the west side. And after supper I told my mother I was going over to stay with my grandmother.

So we were supposed to meet at the pool. The train left about 11:00 o'clock so we were going to meet at 10:30 at the poolhall on the corner of 12th and Center. And I went there and Alvin Snyder didn't show up. So now I'm stuck, I don't know what to do. Bill's got my horn. So I ran into another friend of mine who did this thing all the time, his name was Clifford Finney. I said, 'Clifford, I -- you know, I told him the story. He said, 'don't worry, I'll go with you.'
So we go down and this train pulled out. We jumped

onto the coal tender and pulled right on out of Des Moines toward Chicago. Well, when we get to Rock Island, that's where they changed engines. Well, he knew the whole thing, to get off and we waited and when they hooked a new engine on to start out, we got back on again.

So by the time we came into Chicago, we got off at the Englewood Station, so we jump off because that's where Bill was going to get off. And we waited until the train passed and as the train passed, two policemen jumped off the train and grabbed us. And they said they had information that two kids had come in on this train. So we said, "no, we didn't come on the train, we were just come over to meet a friend." By that time Bill saw us and he came over and rescued us.
Those must have been some anxious moments.

So Clifford, he turns right around and catches the next train back to Des Moines, and I go on with Bill up to the apartment that he had there. It was like a refuge for all Des Moines kids and he was chief cook. And he kept this apartment and all the kids that came from Des Moines would always go stay at his place. And he would come home and cook, cream of tomato soup, and all that. And anyway, I went on up there.
So now I'm in Chicago. So I'm going around to listen to different people, music and all that. But I was too young
to get into the nightclubs. Louis was playing, Louis Armstrong was playing at the Plantation.
That's when he came back from Fletcher's band?

Yeah, he was playing -- this was 1927. And he was playing at the Plantation. But I did meet him, actually, at the Warwick Ballroom on 47th Street. On Sunday afternoon they was playing a dance there. But now [unintelligible] I had an opportunity to try out for a band which was called the "Society Syncopaters." And before the rehearsal we had a jam session and everybody was so thrilled with me because, you know, I was playing all the Coleman Hawkins stuff, and alto at that time, you know.

So now the leader was happy, he was going to get me a job with the band. So now the rehearsal started. Well then they found out I couldn't read. So the leader was very nice. He said to me, "well, you play very good but you've got to learn how to read." But, he said, I have a man that maybe can help you out. So he gave me the phone number and address of a man, a piano player named Bill Fry.

Well, I met Bill Fry and Bill Fry was a piano player that played by ear. And he played all the house rent parties -- we called them chittling struts then. And they played all the house rent parties on the weekend around Chicago. So he took me with him and we would play maybe 10 or 15 of these

from Friday night over to Sunday, we'd play about 10 or 15 of them, just go from one to the other, all day long Saturday and all night Saturday night. And just play from one house rent party to the other. And the fellow would give us -- pay us a dollar and give us a plate of food like chittlings or fried chicken, or something like that. And they gambled and they danced, you know, in these apartments. And he'd let us make three passes on the crap table, you know. By that we would make ourselves five or six, maybe ten dollars in each place. Then Sunday morning we'd end up on Cottage Avenue. They had a place over there called the Ellis Apartments, at some chick's apartment having hot grits and bacon and eggs. So we had a ball then and we'd have ourselves $50 or $60.00 in our pocket. And that's the way we did it.
Of course, before I had met him I had gotten me a job, I was working at the Hammond Stockyards trucking ice, and I didn't stay out there very long. But it was something to hold me together.

So one day I get a telegram from a band called the Virginia Ravens. And that was a territory band that was travelling through Iowa and playing one-nighters through Iowa and Illinois and Minnesota and Wisconsin. And the telegram read that they had passed through Des Moines and I was recommended highly and they wanted a saxophone player that could read, fake and improvise. And ~ the character and all that.

So Bill said, "man, there's your opportunity." I said, "look, they said you've got to read." He says, "man, you could make it. Go ahead anyway." So now I had in the meantime pawned my saxophone for something and I didn't have a horn. So he said, "go anyway." So anyway, I wrote -- sent them a telegram back that I would come and they sent me a ticket.
They were in Des Moines at the time?
No, they were out in Genessee, Illinois, G-e-n-e-s-s-e, I think. They were out there so I got this ticket and I hopped on the train and went out there.
(Well)

I got into that town about 8:00 o'clock at night and all the band with the bus met me at the station and we had to open a dance at 8:30. So they were so thrilled to get -- they thought, you know, a fellow from Chicago, you know, they thought that they were happy to get me.

So when I got there the first thing I said was, "well, I didn't have a horn." They said, "don't worry, we got a (unintelligible). What do you want to play, alto or tenor?" Well, I had missed up with alto playing, I knew the alto player had to play the first part. So I said, I'll play tenor. So they gave me a tenor.
Had you played a tenor before?
No, I hadn't played tenor, but I had the tenor idea from listening to Coleman Hawkins and I heard Slim Freeman who came to Des Moines with this Midnight

Ramblers from Chicago and they were playing all the Fletcher Henderson arrangements. Well, Slim was -- but that's my whole build-up, was wanting to be a tenor player in the first place, you know, from listening to Hawkins, Slim. And I'll tell you the story.

But anyway, I went in this band playing tenor and we played for about two weeks before we could have a rehearsal. Well, I had a good ear so I played tenor. The first saxophone player was named Bill Crump, who's living in California now. And the third saxophone player, I can never remember his name. But he played violin, he was also a barber.

But anyway, I played with them and our conductor was named Lee Langster. He was from Chicago. He was an older man. You know how kids are, these were all teenage kids and they were all, naturally by the leader being older, they all isolated themselves off from the leader, you know. Because he was like a schoolmaster, you know.

So we played for two weeks and in this two weeks being the tenor player I got all the solos, and I was breaking up the crowd everywhere we played. I had stolen out of the trick that Slim Freeman had done, laying on his back and turning the horn upside down and all this stuff, and slapped alonguing and all that. And I'd become the star in the band.
Meanwhile, how were you doing with the reading?
I was faking.
You heard the part?
Yeah, I could hear the first part.

And music wasn't as complicated then as it is now. Everything was melody so all you had to do was hear the melody and follow right along with it, like singing, you know. They only had three horns, too, so it wasn't too difficult.

So one day we were in some little town and the leader called a rehearsal. So we had this rehearsal and I'll never forget the orchestration he put up, it was called "Sam, Sam, the accordion man." And this thing had a six bar -- eight bar introduction. And naturally, after the six bar the tenor saxophone break. And in those days when you had a break the band always stopped. Well, when they stopped at the end of the six bars, I stopped, too.

He said, "You've got a tenor break there." So I said okay, and they started again. And I flew into one of my things. He stopped the band again and he said, "it's written there what you're supposed to play." And there I was, shown up right away. And he said, "you mean to tell me you've been sitting in this band all the time and you couldn't read?" I said, well, yes, sir, that's the way it's been." And I had already told Bill Crump, the first man, that I couldn't read but he didn't believe it. He always said, oh, man, you Chicagoans are always putting people on.

So then right away he said, 'well, I'm going to have to fire you because, I mean, we have to have somebody that can read.' So I started packing my horn up and I started off the bandstand and the people that owned the band were two Jewish people, the Faths, Mr. Howard Fath.
F-a-t-h?

Yeah. And he said, Eddie, where are you going? And he said, well, aren't you going to rehearse? I said, 'Oh, no, Lee just fired me.' He said, 'well, they can't fire you, you're our star. You put your horn together and go back on the bandstand.'

So I did and when I got back he looked at me and said, 'what are you coming back for?' And I said, 'well, Mr. Fath said you can't fire me.' He said, 'no, he's our attraction.' So he said, 'well then, I'll have to teach you how to read.' So to make it short, Lee sat with me about an hour a day for the next couple of weeks and taught me how to read. It wasn't very difficult.
So then after I learned how to read they put me on alto and put Bill on tenor. Then I had to play first. And I was stuck playing first the rest of my life because I was a good reader, you know.
I know you told me the night we were (unintelligible) you know, because you were playing tenor there and you'd always wanted to play tenor
Right.
And you always had to play alto.

The other saxophone player said, 'well -- I've got a summer job up in Madison, Wisconsin with a fellow out of Fort Wayne named Don Phillips. Would you like to come along and play first saxophone? When we were with the Ravens, they paid $5.00 a night. And in those days you could get a room for 50 cents a night, if you doubled up it was 25 cents. And you could get a steak dinner for 35 cents, so I used to save $3.00 a week. But this job in Madison they said, we'll pay you $60.00 a week. Well, gosh, that was something for a kid in those days because the average man's salary, the average working man was $15.00, $20.00 a week.
So he and I put in our notice and we went up to Madison to play with this band, with Don Phillips.
That was Madison, Wisconsin?

Madison, Wisconsin. So Lee Langster, the leader and I have become such good friends. And since I became his friend all the guys had gotten close to him. He didn't stay in the band after that, he just quit and went back to Chicago. I never heard of him again.

But anyway, we went to Madison and we played with Don at a place out there in Madison called the Broadway Gardens. And we stayed there all summer. Well, the band was composed of mostly the fellows from Pittsburgh. And Don

Phillips was from Fort Wayne and then I came and Charlie Lee was the tenor player. He died a few years ago, but he was kind of prominent. And then they had Byron Garrison who later became -- he was on banjo, he later became a saxophone player. And they had Robert Murray on trombone, Don Phillips was playing the piano. And we stayed up in Madison all that year.

Well, being kids, and we didn't drink or anything, we used to have so much money we would go out to the drug store and see who could drink up the most malted milks and things like that. But this job lasted all summer and when the summer job broke up the boys went back to Pittsburgh. And I, the closest place I knew to go was to Milwaukee. I had a cousin over in Milwaukee and she lived there so I just went on over to Milwaukee to stay with her a while.

And while I was in Milwaukee, one day I was walking down to the place called the Metropole there, where the musicians hung out. And I walked down there and there was the Virginia Ravens' bus. So I walked over and the guys was glad to see me and they gave me my job back. So I went on back with them and I stayed -- we played around there with them all -- somewhere up in Wisconsin, Eau Claire and Black River Falls and all that. And finally they needed a trumpet player. Well, I found this boy, Leroy White, he was down in Pittsburgh, Kansas playing with Walter Thomas and a bunch of them,

Jameson's band down in Wichita. And I got him and Joe Thomas, who was Walter Thomas' brother, to come up from there to play with the Virginia Ravens. And then also Merle Williams was home, he came back with the Virginia Ravens.
Now, this is Joe Thomas the tenor player?
Not the one with Jimmy Lunceford. He was an alto player, Joe Thomas. He's here in New York now. He's a writer, he's with --
(End of side one as recorded.)

Joe Thomas was the alto player but he was Walter Foots Thomas' brother. And they had all been together down in Wichita. So they came and joined the Virginia Ravens. And then Merle left and a piano player out of Springfield, Missouri, I think that's right -- now, Springfield, Illinois, named Frank Hines. He took put Merle's place. And Frank was a marvelous piano player, he played something like Earl Hines. So we were with the Virginians and Frank used to say to me, "Eddie, you play a great jazz saxophone. But, he said, you don't know your chords." So I said chords, what do you mean?" So he started telling me about the C7, B flat 7, F7. So he says, I'm going to buy you a record.
So he bought me a record of Frankie Trumbauer Trombaer singing the Blues." And I fell in love with that style so I started buying all the things that Frankie Trumbauer made, that he made
with Bix and Ed Lang and Miff Mole and Jimmy Dorsey, different ones. But I bought everything because of Frankie Trumbauer. And I learned his style on alto.

Then I bought me a banjo book, A McNeills (PHONETIC) Banjo book, and learned the cycle of the 5th, and chords, and I practiced all these on my saxophone. So now this improved my playing very much. Then I got interested in writing and I started to write a little bit, you know.
But anyway, along -- we played with the Virginia Ravens all that summer.
So now you're into December what, '28?

'27. And we all left the Virginia Ravens, seven of us left at once, Roy, the trumpet player left, we had a tenor saxophone player named Birdson, and I left. And Edgar Pillows had come in, I had gotten him a job playing bass in the band. He left with us. In fact, we just quit, all of us. Connie Landers, that was the banjo player, he quit. And so when they left us in Shell Lake, Wisconsin, they only had about three men left. That was the drummer and Joe Thomas and somebody else, because Bill Crump had gone before because I was playing.
Anyway, we decided to go to Minneapolis, the seven of us. So we bought our tickets, we got on the train and we were headed out to Minneapolis. And we run into a gangster

named Red Kelly from St. Louis. He came up and saw us sitting on the train, we all had our instruments. He says, 'you guys musicians?' Yeah, we said. He said, 'well, get those horns out, you can't make no money sitting on your fanny, you know.' So we got our horns out and we started playing on the train. So he passed the hat up and down the train, come back with a lot of money, you know.

He said, 'where you going?' We said, Minneapolis. He said, 'well, would you mind detouring and going with me for a few days?' We said, 'no, we don't mind, we have nowhere to go.' We'd never been to Minneapolis before, anyway.

So he said, 'well, I'll make your tickets and things and I'll send you off to Minneapolis when we get through.' So he took us up to a resort in Iowa, Grand View, Iowa. And we went up there and he took us up there for a birthday present for some party he was going to. Then they set us up and put us in cabins and everything.

They had a band, so they said, 'well, this night --' he said, 'I have a band here that will outplay your band.' And they put up money and bet. And we won it and they gave us the money. So they kept us there about three or four days. And when we left we all had about $75.00 or $80.00 a piece when we left there.
So then we went on to Minneapolis.
Seems like in those days things just

So we go on to Minneapolis and when we got into Minneapolis we all got our places and we organized a band there called the Ethiopian Symphonians. And it was ten pieces, we had three saxs; I was playing alto and we had a big guy named Pete Richardson playing alto and the tenor player was a fellow named Jack Bradley. And he tried to play everything like Coleman Hawkins. And we had Roy White, later they called him Snake White, had him on trumpet. And --
Who was the leader of the band?
Well, it was just a bunch of --
(Inaudible).

Yeah. We had a drummer named Mo Strange and a bass player named Willy Burrell and Connie Ladders was playing banjo. And Frank Hines was on the piano. And so now I began to write a little bit. We were playing all of Fletcher Henderson's records. Now, through the study of these chords and things I'd started to write a little bit. It took me a month to make an arrangement but I finally would get the part down. And it got better and better and I was writing arrangements. And we were rehearsing. Some of the things we couldn't write we would listen and learn. So we were playing all of Fletcher Henderson --
Right off the records?

Yeah, right from the records. And this band, we played around there with Minneapolis for, oh, maybe four or five months, whatever it was. And finally a fellow named Clarence Johnson who had a -- was a piano player, he got a job up in a hotel up in Bismark, North Dakota for the winter at the Spencer Hotel. And so he took me and Snake, the trumpet player, Roy White, and the banjo player, Landers. And he had a drummer from St. Paul, which I don't remember his name, five pieces and we went up to Bismark.
What do they do in the winter in Bismark, North Dakota?

Well, this was 55 below zero weather up there that winter. But this hotel we played in, the Spencer was right on the corner. And then they had an annex where we stayed and we didn't have to go outdoors to go to -- we only played two hours a day, that was from 6:00 to 8:00 for the dinner hour. And that's all we had to do. And the job paid $30.00 a week.

So we were stationed now -- in this annex where we were stationed was stationed Lester Young's father -- had his family band. Lester Young and his little brother Lee, he wasn't big enough to play then. But they'd dress him in a tuxedo and he would conduct the band. And Irma, his sister, was the saxophone player and the mother would play the piano

player and his father would play tenor. Lester was playing alto. But he was learning to play then, you know, and he said he used to -- so anyway, I had my records, my Trombone records, and I used to play them.

One day I heard a knock on the door. I hadn't met him then, but I heard a knock on the door and he opened the door. "I'm Lester Young," he says. "I hear that little saxophone. Who is that playing saxophone? I said, Frankie Trumbauer. He said, well, do you mind if I listen? So he came in and we met, you know. And he started to borrow these records. And he used to tell me he had an old, beat-up alto but one of these days when he learned how to read good his father was going to buy him a new Selmer (PHONETIC).
So we became good friends there and he used to come over everytime he had a chance, when they weren't out.
This is the winter of '28?

Still in '27. Because all of this happened, you know -- but we stayed over through into '28. And through the winter. And that next spring we left Bismark and came back to -- I came to Minneapolis with this group. And then I got me, finally organized me a little band. In fact, Roy was the trumpet player, and myself -- I have the letterheads at home now, called -- we got together and organized a little group called the Doo Dads from Ditty Wah Ditty. Now, where the name come -- in those days they used to have

a comic strip called the Doo Dads. I know you don't remember it, but it was these little people like the Seven Dwarfs. And that word Ditty Wah Ditty was a slang word, we used to say, you know, if you're going to some place out of the world called Ditty Wah Ditty. So we named our little band the Doo Dads from Ditty Wah Ditty.

And we got a job playing for a dance marathon up in MINOCWA Minopie- (DUNNETTE) Wisconsin. Of course, before then Lester Young had left his father's band and came to Minneapolis playing tenor. And that's when he and I used to get together, just the two of us, and play school dances just with the sax es alto and tenor and no rhythm or nothing. Just played the two of us.
That was in '28?

Yeah, in the spring. So we got this little band, it was Roy White and Jimmy Farris on trombone and I was playing alto. And Leon Lewis was the drummer. And we had Merle Williams again on piano. I have pictures of him. And a fellow named Charlie Odin on bass, playing tuba. MINOCWA

So we went up to Menocwa, Wisconsin to play for a dance marathon, you know, they had in those days. You played and then you took a rest but these people danced around the clock, you know. And while we were in Menocwa, Wisconsin, Leroy Rice from Milwaukee came through with his band. They had guys like Jimmy Dudley and all those guys with his group. And he had a ten piece band but he heard our seven pieces; had

Connie Landers on banjo. He heard our seven pieces and he liked us. So he asked us, would we join him. We said, yes. So he took his ten piece band back to Milwaukee, brought his bus up there and took our seven pieces. Because we were playing all this trombone stuff at that time.

No, we had switched now because we had the typical combination for this stuff, the trombone, and we were playing all that kind of stuff at that time. So he took us, and his band took us back to Milwaukee.

Then there was another band in Milwaukee at that time called Grant Moore and His New Orleans Black Devils and there was another band there called Tommy Fox's band. He was a drummer. And there was a band on the Roof Garden, Arthur Simms and his Wisconsin Roof Orchestra which later became Bernie Young's orchestra.

They were playing at the Wisconsin Roof Ballroom. See, because in those days there was a ballroom every place you went, they had a ballroom and a house band. And the road bands would come in and play opposite them in 15 minute sets. And usually the dances were from 8:30 to [illegible] 11:30.
So then we played around there mostly of that winter.

And naturally we had jam sessions and things afterwards, when guys like Eddie Inge and Jimmy Dudley and those guys used to jam. There was a very fine saxophone player in Milwaukee that never did leave there, only to go to Minneapolis, named Earl Keith. He played great alto and great saxophone. He reminded you of guys like Charlie Parker, really great. But he never left, he stayed out that way.

But Jimmy Dudley left and went to the Cotton Pickers. First he went to Billy Minor in Detroit and then he went to the Cotton Pickers. So anyway, we played around Milwaukee that winter and then we finally -- then I finally left there and we went to Minneapolis to play for the Stecker Brothers. And in that interim I had this -- I was playing from one band -- I played with Eli a while and then I'd play with Grant Moore a while, except for the time we got snowbound up there. And after switching from band to band and going to Minneapolis and playing with these, you know, different -- because both of these bands played both Minneapolis and Milwaukee. So we switched from one to the other.

Then I had -- I was always itchy to go someplace so I wrote a fellow up in Toledo had a band called Frank Terry's Chicago Nightengales, I think it was. And I wrote them a letter and they sent for me and I went up there as his musical director and arranger and saxophone player. And this is where I met Art Tatum. Art Tatum was -- I was living on

City Park, right across the street from Art. And one night we played with the house band at the Recreation Ballroom there. And we would play five nights or six nights a week and on Monday we'd have off and we'd give a colored dance.

So this one night we -- I'm ahead of myself, because before that I had gone -- before this I -- Eddie Inge had left the Milwaukee band, the Roof Garden. And they sent for me, to Minneapolis, to come and play with them on the Wisconsin Roof. Then we went to Chicago and played that winter. And we went to Chicago and played at the Savoy Ballroom the rest of that winter and all that summer with Bernie Young's band.
That was 1929?

No, this is now 1930. And we were the house band at the Savoy Ballroom and that's when I really got the chance to meet Louis because he came there to play a couple of times. And then this trumpet player who I had met in 1926 in --
Coming out of Pittsburgh?

Yeah, Sid Valentine or Raymond Valentine, he joined us at Bernie Young's band and also Doc Wheeler who was Wheeler Moran, that's his real name. He's called Doc Wheeler now, he was a disc jockey. Well, he joined the band on trombone.
But at that time he was so bashful. He used to have a wonderful singing voice but he was so bashful he'd sit down

to sing, you know. But he'd sing and the band would play trombone. And Raymond Valentine was a crack trumpet player. He was one of the trumpet players that Louis really listened to. He'd come up and say to him -- they'd go opposite at the Savoy and Louis had to pat him on the back because a great trumpet player. But he finally got along the wayside later.
Never recorded?

No, I don't think so. And then we took that band, after we finished the Savoy that summer, we went down to Tulsa, Oklahoma to work. And that's where I ran into Alphonso Trent again and he had Hayes Pillars on tenor and Stuff Smith (PHONETIC) on violin.

And then we came back and then I went back to Minneapolis. And I think that's when I had Herschel Evans to come up and play with Grant Moore and he played with Grant Moore out to the -- we were stationed in Sioux City. Then I joined Eli Rice again because Bert Bailey was playing with him and he got sick. And I went back to Minneapolis. And then after that, that's when I went to Toledo. This is 1931.
Just for the record, you're talking about Hayes Pillars who later had the Jester-Pillars Orchestra?
Right.
And the other fellow you're talking about was Edgar Pillows?
Edgar Pillows, yeah, that was a different man. He was a bass player.
Yeah, but that was P-i-l-l-o-w-s?
Right. So then I went to Toledo. And one night we were playing this colored dance, as I said before.
On Monday night?

Yeah. So at the intermission I was going out, get a little air, you know, have a little taste. So Frank Terry says to me, wait a minute, I want you to hear something? I said, what do you want me to hear? He says, I want you to hear a piano player. I said, man, I don't want to hear no piano player, I've heard all the greats, I heard Earl Hines when I was in Chicago, and Casno Simpson (phonetic) he played in Bernie Young's band, Casno Simpson, we had two pinaos. We had Burdett's Loving Good and Casno Simpson on (unintelligible) and both of them were crack piano players, you know. And Casno played the same style that Earl Hines played and he was really a great jazz piano player. So I wasn't interested.

So as I was just about to go out the door I heard this crescendo on the piano. They brought this kid up on the bandstand, led him up on the bandstand and I heard this great crescendo on the piano and I turned around and went back. And it was Art Tatum. And he started out playing Tiger Rag, right

off the bat. And this I had to acknowledge, you know. So then I met Art Tatum and we became friends. He used to live right across the street from me. I lived right across the street from him, rather, in Toledo in City Park.

And he had a grand collection of Earl Hines records. That was his favorite piano player at that time. And so then I stayed around Toledo with this band all that summer and I played with Art and I played with Teddy Wilson at the Chateau of France because we had a little group. It was Art Tatum that we used to run around. We were all teenagers and we had a little group like -- of course, that was 1931, I was 21 years old at that time. And we ran together after we got off from our respective jobs.
How did Teddy Wilson get there?

He was there. I don't know how he got there but he was there. So Teddy -- we had a good gang. It was Teddy Wilson, Art Tatum and Art was playing at Nobles, Teddy was playing the Chateau de France, and myself and another saxophone player named George White. He's Skippy White's father, the drummer here. And there was a tenor player out of Detroit named Adams. And then Ben Smith --not Ben Smith but Ben Richardson, who was clarinet player. And he's here in New York now. We had a little gang that we used to run around and hit all the joints at night and drink moonshine, and you know.
So this is how -- and played, you know. Jam and play and all hang out together. And that's when Art and I became very good friends, and Teddy Wilson. We all were good friends.
Had you run into Coleman Hawkins by this time?

I hadn't seen my idol yet, you know. But in the meantime I picked up on Benny Carter who I felt was the greatest alto player, you know. Because then I started thinking I liked Benny Carter. I started to try to play him, emulate, you know, tried to pick up his style of playing because after him, I think, I graduated from Trombauer to Benny Carter who today I still think is the greatest all around alto player in the world. Because he set the style for lead playing and he set the style for all these things.

So anyway, I stayed around there and then finally I went on back to Minneapolis. And I stayed around Minneapolis until finally I'd get a call, telegram to come to Chicago to play with Ralph Cooper at the Regal Theater.
This was Ralph Cooper who was in the movies?
Right, right.
And later on the radio?
Uh-huh. So I go over to play with Raoul because previously when I had been in Chicago before,

when I was with Bernie Young, I used to go often across the street to the Metropolitan Theater to hear Erskine Tate's band, to listen to Omar Simeon because there was another great clarinet and great saxophone player. Because I always went to hear the saxophone players, mostly.

But anyway, I went to Chicago to play with Ralph Cooper in the Regal Theater, and by him bringing me from Minneapolis there, they fired the whole band off the job. So Ralph Cooper and Reginald Forsythe who was writing for Earl Hines, we were all cooped up together at the Oakwood Boulevard there, that hotel was called, I think, the Ritz -- the Tremier (PHONETIC) Hotel it was called then, right next to the Grand Terrace on Oakwood Boulevard.

So all the folks bunked up there together in this room. And so I had some arrangements and I had never written for over one trombone at that time. So I just took an ad, Earl Hines had two trombones. So I added another trombone part to my (SOPRANO SAX) (UNINTELLIGIBLE), took him over for Earl to play and they sounded terrible with this other added trombone part and I couldn't figure it out. So Reginald Forsythe, he showed me how to VOICE the trombones so they wouldn't -- I just added the part, and that's how I first learned how to space the brass out, from him.
So now while I'm there with them, Benny Moten's band comes to Chicago, playing on the North Side. And I ran

into Ben Webster and naturally, he being the jazz player he invited me out to the theater. And we had a big jam session out at the theater. So Benny Moten said, why don't you come on to go -- I'm making some changes in the band, why don't you come on and go to Kansas City. I said, of course, because I wasn't doing nothing.

So Macleo Burchell was his manager. We all drove on in his car, his Ford. And they had their bus, or whatever it is, and we went to Kansas City. And Benny revamped his band. I was put on lead alto with Ben Webster and Jack Washington. And we had Eddie Durham on banjo -- on guitar and trombone. And we had Dan Minor on trombone. And we had Hot Lips Paige. And at that time we had Joe Smith, Russell Smith's brother on trumpet and Hot Lips Paige and Joe Keyes. He was my roommate. And gee, Joe, he was playing first. And we had -- Buster Moten was conducting the orchestra and playing guitar. And Count Bassie was on the piano, it was Bill Bassie then. And Benny Moten used to play piano occasionally. We used to have two pianos occasionally. And Buster -- guitar, Buster Berry on guitar. And Willy Mae Washington on the drums and Walter Paige on the bass.

Of course, I knew Walter Paige before because when I was in Sioux City, Iowa, stationed there with Grant Moore, the Blue Devils were stationed there, too. They were playing in Sioux City and they had Lester Young and Buster Smith and
Theodore Ross was playing lead alto. And Lester Young and all of them were there in Sioux City at that time.

So anyway, we went back to Kansas City and we started rehearsing this new band. And we stayed around there a while. Finally we took another trip back out East. And we were stranded all over the United States. Everywhere this band -- we had a lot of fun but we never really made any money. We were stranded everyplace. We played --
What was the reason for getting stranded so many places? Promoters wouldn't pay?

Sometimes the promoter wouldn't -- sometimes the guys would run off with the money after the intermission and leave us. Oh, a lot of things happened. So we were stranded in Zanesville, we were stranded in Columbus, Ohio, we were stranded in Cincinnati.
This is 1932?

This is 1932. And we were stranded in Philadelphia. In fact, the story of Philadelphia is a crack up. We had played all these places and stranded from place to place. So finally we're getting into Philadelphia and we're going to play the Pearl Theater. And that was run by Steiffel, Sam Steiffel. Now we're going to play there a week. We'd never had a week stand any place. So we were going to play there a week with chorus girls, and they had this Ristina Banks (PHONETIC) number one chorus there playing with us.

But now, the night we got into Philly, we were going to open the next day, Fletcher Henderson's band was rehearsing there to go to New York. And that's when I first came face to face with Coleman Hawkins. And I was so thrilled, you know, to see Coleman Hawkins in person. And we -- so anyway, we opened there that next day. And we were so happy that we were going to get a week's salary at the end of the week we just had a ball, you know, we would tab our room, we'd tab food, tab our whiskey. We was having a ball the whole week.

So anyway, at the end of the week we were lined up to get paid and Benny tells us that the last time they had been out there in Philly working, Sam Steiffel had lent them money to buy uniforms and he owed him that money. So they attached the box office and took all the money.

So the next morning there we stood out, the whole band out in front of the Pearl Theater, with our bags and our horns but no bus. They took the bus and everything. So there we stood out in front there.

So finally Benny goes off and he finds a guy named Archie who's a colored guy, promoter. And they got a big old bus and took us over to Camden, New Jersey. And took us to a poolhall and this guy took a tub and took one rabit and made a big stew. And we got bread, a lot of bread, and stood around and sopped up this stew and ate this gravy. I always called it cat stew because I didn't figure out where this guy got

this rabbit.
(Laughter.)
I'd always kid him and say that we ate cat stew that day. And then we went over to the church and recorded that famous album which has been re-released and re-released and we never did get paid for that, either. In fact, I have a tune that I wrote on there and arranged, never did get anything out of it.
Which was that?

Toby." So that -- so after we played Philly we finally went to Newport News and fooled around. Finally the band made our way back to Kansas City. Then I was pretty well fed up so I wrote to Zach White in Columbus, Ohio and he sent for me and I went out to Columbus, Ohio to join Zach White. And Sy Oliver was there in the band.
What was the difference from the Moten band, you know, from the other bands you'd been playing with? That Kansas City thing, did you recognize the variations in styles?

Well, the reason I didn't recognize any variation was because I took a lot to that band. But you see, being the lead alto player, we had Eddie Durham was doing most of the writing. I did some writing. A lot of our stuff was done by ear and by head and I used to set all of the rhythmic passage -- patterns for the saxophone section, which they
didn't do previous to that. And that style is what hung over to the Count Basie band, see.

But I was responsible for most all the riffs that the saxophone played. And sometimes Hot Lips Paige would come out and play on the end and play, maybe sometimes according to how he felt, he might play 50 choruses on the end of St. Louis Blues. And I would set a different pattern in each chorus. And Ben and Jack would pick it up and we would go on, you know, and keep building --
That built the momentum?
Right.
What about, you know, as far as rhythm sections. Was there a difference? Between those bands and the other bands playing then?
No, the only difference in the rhythm section of that band was the bass player, a string bass. Before most of the bands I played with had tubas.
You mean Grant Moore and all those other bands?
Yeah, they all had tubas. And this was a different thing. You had the string bass helping the rhythm section.
But see in those days, everybody didn't just depend on the rhythm section. Every man played with a beat. I remember, in fact, when Jimmy Lunceford was here, when they

recorded, they'd have to put a pillow under Willie Smith's foot so he didn't jar the microphone because he was patting his foot so loud. And most of the bands in those days, when you went to a dance you could hear the feet on the dance floor. Everybody was beating in time, it was one of those things you could hear the patting of the feet right along with the music. And this made a lot of the momentum in the swing more predominant. See, because everybody played with a beat. Today nobody plays together with a beat. You've got a rhythm section and every man is playing his own thing. Where in those days we'd have section rehearsals. You had the rhythm rehearsal, piano, drums, bass and guitar. They had a separate rehearsal. The Brass section had a separate rehearsal and reeds had a separate rehearsal. Then we'd put it together. And everybody had a thing going with the bass hand and the piano and the bass would be together. And the bass drum and -- it was all WORKED whipped out together.

I remember many a fight between the bass player and the drummer about who was right and who was wrong. Well today, nobody plays together. Everybody has got his own little thing and I think that DISTURBS the rhythm or the beat. Because everything predominantly in those days was played for people to dance by.
So the worst dancer in the audience could tell when the band got off, you know.
You don't say there was a general Midwestern or Southwestern style?

No, I don't. That's one of the things, the biggest fallacies that I ever heard in my life was West Coast style, as far as jazz is concerned. West Coast style, Chicago style and New York style, because all of the same guys were playing it. You know, a guy would come to New York and everybody was playing together.

Now, if you want to get into something else like out in Iowa where it was predominantly hillbillies and everything playing "Turkey in the Straw," I broke my teeth on it. But when it comes down to jazz, this thing was a universal thing. Even in Europe that's all they learn how to play, listening to records.
I meant, you know, were the nuances, things, different?

All I can say is jazz evolved as it went. You might say we started with ragtime and went through the 20's with the jazz era, which is swing, which was really swing then. Because it always did swing, but they --
The name with a capital "S"? (Unintelligible) less?
Yeah. So when Benny Goodman came in they called it swing, but he only was swinging the things that Fletcher Henderson was swinging in the twenties.
I guess -- you know, you saying that
you learned from records and all that, Henderson's band and Trumbower and whatever, so once records came in and people were able to buy records --

Right. And then you learn from each other as you went, and those same guys had to learn from listening to records. So everybody learned from each other. And that's the way the whole thing did. But I think the critics and a lot of people that weren't musicians, that write the books and things, they put these cliches on jazz and bebop and all that. It's just the evolution of jazz and the thing just kept on evolving from the way I used to play it by ear until the way -- then I began to learn about chords and harmony and learn how to use these tools to play. And then like they started with -- I said before, many kinds of combinations. Finally they had a set combination for a ten piece band with two trumpets, and a trumpet and two altos and the tenor. Then they finally added on another tenor then they finally added another -- in fact the first -- when I joined Cab Calloway he only had two altos and a tenor and when he added me he had three altos and a tenor, see.

And then eventually the thing became a standard style where they had two altos, two tenors and a baritone. And the trumpet started doing it. But it was an evolution. But everybody was still playing the same thing but it was just getting to be a more involved harmonic thing from playing

chords to utilizing the whole scale in your playing. And harmonization. Where before we played just three part harmony. Along about 1928 McKinney's Cotton Pickers came in adding the sixth. And this was an evolution. In fact, when I added the sixth to our chords out there in Minneapolis, the leader wouldn't play those arrangements because he said they sounded bad. And McKinney's Cotton Pickers started this and when Don Redman came in they started using five brass and six, you know, like that. So it got even Paul Whiteman's band in the twenties, he had a big band but they never bothered with anything more than three part harmony.
Just doubling up?

Yeah, that's right. But now -- because that was the classical sound. But guys like John Nesbit and Don Redman started this, adding the sixth and then everybody started doing it. And they started using more pieces. Then they started adding the ninth and all of that and the 13th and 11th and everything in the chords.

So then the boppers did that, started using the augmented 11th. So finally they were using the whole scale. And they still haven't finished yet but someone cut the whole thing off around the 1940's. In the forties they cut the whole thing off and went back to the beginning again with the triads and church harmony with the rock. And a lot of the

rhythm and blues stuff.
So the people that controlled the business stopped us. Because we can still go farther yet with harmony and everything. And as I say, the people, ordinary names here, it gets a little bit complicated unless there are people that really follow music, you know. When you start listening to more than three horns and things, you just start to get so involved that you can't keep it all together. So that's why today most of the people are interested mostly in solos, you know.

Sure.

and the Jabbo Smiths and the Louis Armstrongs and all of these trumpet players, Dizzy Gillespies and Charlie Shaffers. I mean, this was the thing.
