holding a trombone in the picture. But that's how we got that picture.
Well, that's typical of Hollywood logic, you know. You're a reed player and you're holding a trombone. How'd they figure that out?
Well, that was the only thing for me to do, I guess. Because everything else in the band was filled out. So anyway, that's how we got this picture.

And then after that I -- we played down -- I took my band down -- before that we had taken our band to Santa Monica and played around there. So then after I was working in the studio awhile, it was 1938, I was itching to come back to New York anyway and Fletcher Henderson's band came out.

Okay, before we get to that, what was it like in California in those years, besides the jobs that you were working? I mean, what else were you doing? What was the jamming scene, what was the after hours scene like?

California wasn't like New York. My thing -- see, when I first stayed out to California I stayed out there with -- of course, I had gotten an ulcer and stomach and I had to leave Cab's band to stay out there to have medication. And I was offered a job to work in the Club Alabam with Lorenzo Pornoy (PHONETIC). Well, after Cab and them left, that first night in there the delegate, who's name is Elmer Faine, he and I became good friends after that, came

over and wouldn't let me work. So the job only payed $22.50 a week but at that time I had a four room house that I -- with a garage, and rented furnished for $20.00 a month. So anyway, after he wouldn't let me work, said I had to put my card in, I just took my horn home and shined it up nice and put it in the case and put it right under the bed. And I started making -- I had a car and I started going out to the Palladium and meeting all the bands and writing for them. Red Norvelle and Jimmy Dorsey and all these different bands, and I was making myself about $300.00 a week. And the guys couldn't understand this. A lot of guys used to say to me in California at the time, "what are you staying out here for? I thought you'd go back to New York." But I was making more money than they were making so I stayed.
Then I finally decided to organize a band and I organized the band and I put the secretary of the union on baritone sax and everything worked out beautiful.
Well, what about the extra-curricular thing. You know, what was the scene like? Where did you go after the gig? Was there still --

Oh, there wasn't too many places out there. Well, we did -- now, during the time I was out there Art Tatum came out there, Stuff Smith came out there with his band, with Cozy Cole and Clyde Hart and Mack -- Jonah Jones. And they were playing at a place called The Famous Door.

Now, when they came out there we used to go out at night with Stuff and me and Clyde and Jonah and all of them. We used to go around places like after hour spots and we would jam and play. And this is one of the big things that made Stuff mess up his career because when he first came out there Stuff was very hot. He'd come from 52nd Street and they had pictures lined up and everything for him to do. And we were hanging out after they got off.

So one night we was out and we were all kind of juiced up and we started kidding Stuff because Stuff had just gotten married and we was kidding him about some guy being out with his wife. And the next day Stuff left and went back to New York and left the band out there. So I took his place with the band. And played with them for two weeks before Stuff came back. And when Stuff came back he had to play -- I'd displaced him, you know, to make up for what he left there. And he lost the movies and he had to stay out there and play for practically nothing to make up for what they said he'd made the place lose by his not being there.
But we did used to hang out and go and play. When they came out there. Not many of the California guys did it. All the New York fellows came out and used to go around places and jam.
But the Central Avenue scene really happened later?
Yeah, that was later.
That was wartime.
Yeah, this is before the war.
Anyway, so then you're getting ready to leave California. This is what year?
1938. Well, Fletcher came out. And George Blake wanted to stay in California. So I jumped and joined Fletcher Henderson's band.
Now, had you gotten married or anything?
Oh, yeah.
When did you get married?
Well, I got married in Minneapolis when I was first there, by my first wife. And then --
What year was that?

That was 1930. And then we -- in fact, when I was in Chicago we got married in Chicago. Then while I'm in California, about a year before Fletcher came out there, she and I broke up and she went back to Minneapolis. Then I was single at this time when I joined Fletcher.
That house you had been renting --
Well, I was out of that house by now.
Because you'd broken up?
Yeah, I had a room. And when I went to Chicago with Fletcher Henderson I got married again to my
wife I'm with now. 1938.

But anyway, I joined Fletcher, went to -- well, we played -- in fact, the personnel of the band then was -- the reed section was Hilton Jefferson and myself, Ben Webster and Elmer Williams. And Pop Smith was the trumpet player, Russell Smith and Dick Vance and Emmett Berry were the trumpet players. And Cuffy and the other trombone player, I can't think of his name, was out of Chicago. Naturally, Fletcher was on piano and we had a fellow named Pete Suggs on drums, Israel Crosby on bass and Larry Lucie on guitar.

Then we played the Grand Terrace in Chicago. And my wife, she was in show business. She had been in Hollywood and made pictures. She had made 23 pictures for Cecil B. DeMille and she had just finished making that all-black western, "Harlem on the Prairie" with Herb Jefferies (inaudible). She was the leading lady in there. Her name was --
The Browns
: Buckaroo.
Yeah, her name was Connie Harris. Well, she was working in the show with us in Grand Terrace in Chicago and we met and that's when we got married. And we're still married.

Then I stayed with them at the Grand Terrace. When we finished the Grand Terrace I left Fletcher and came back to New York. Then when I got back to New York I played at the Savoy with Don Redman and then I played -- had my own band

at the Savoy for a while. And then Benny Carter and I got a group. It was Benny Carter's group but I had the book. First I had a band at the Nemo Club with me, Don Byas -- small band, like a John Kirby style band with Don Byas on tenor and I played clarinet. And Otis Johnson on trumpet, Pete Jacobs on drums, Clyde Harte on piano and Bass Hill on bass. We played at the Nemo Club and we played at the -- that was Bill Robinson's place. And we played also at the Elks Rendezvous at the Town. And then we also played at Kelly's Stables downtown.
What year was this, '39?

Around '39, or something like that. And then in '38, the fall of '38, I went and played back with Cab Calloway in Chu's place for about three or four weeks while he had a vacation at the Cotton Club Downtown. I played tenor then.

And then I -- after the Nemo Club then I had this small group's book, Benny Carter and Maxine went to Boston and they used my book. There was Benny Carter and Al Gibson and myself. Benny was playing trumpet and alto. And I was playing clarinet and Al Gibson and Sonny White on piano. And I don't remember who the drummer was.
You said Maxine. Maxine Sullivan?
Maxine Sullivan, yeah. And --
You knew Benny by this time, though?
Oh, yes.
Your paths had crossed many times.

Well, by being with Cab I met everybody. In fact, we used to all hang out around the Harlem at night -- and playing and juicing. Because Harlem was a place where, at that time, every musician, you know -- everybody hung out in certain spots and you ran into everybody. Even the chorus girls, you know, and there was maybe 100 chorus girls up there then.

So then after that I also played at the Savoy with Don Redman. We made records. We made a lot of records while I was in that band. In fact, we did "Mylenberg Joys" (PHONETIC), I did on alto solo on that which the discographers said was Don's solo but it was mine.
With Don Redman?

Yeah. Of course, it's been changed since then. And there's a lot of things that -- in Europe they had me on things with Jelly Roll Morton but I didn't ever play with Jelly Roll. I knew him, met him, but I never played with him.
Well, what was it, the Rhythm Club?
Yeah, the Rhythm Club was right on 132nd and Lenox.
Did you used to hang out there?
Yes, yes. Well, in those days if a
musician was free lancing, black musicians could go up there and get a job every day of the week.
It was like the Exchange?
Yeah. If people wanted black musicians that's where they came to find them.
And then I took a band, my own band at the Savoy for a while.
This is after the Nemo Club?
Yeah.
Was that a big band at the Savoy?

Well, we had about ten pieces. And this was -- in fact, when I was down there playing with Cab in Chu's place, Chick and Bardew Ali, who was his conductor, came down there one night. This is in '39, this is just before he died. And he asked me did I want to come and play clarinet in his band. I said, fine. So he said, we're going on 30 one-nighters. And you can either join now and go with us or join us when we come back. I said, well, I'll join you when you come back. And he died on that trip.
But when the band came back in town I joined the band with Ella.
Ella was in it then?
Yeah. And I played with the band, say, about -- oh, we went out to Chicago, the Grand Terrace. And went out to -- no, we didn't go to California that trip.

We went out on several trips, took several road trips down to Florida and things. We came back and then I quit the band and then I started -- that's when I had the little band, you know, after that. That's when I went to Boston with Benny Carter and --
Maxine Sullivan?

And I come back and I worked with Don Redman in that era somewhere. Then finally one day I was down back of the Apollo Theater and I ran into Charlie Buchanan who had the Savoy. And he said, well, when are you going to come back and work for me. I said, well, I don't want to come back up there but if you want me to do something get me the job conducting for Ella. So he did. He said, meet me down to the office tomorrow. And I went down and (unintelligible) and talked to them and they gave me the job leading the band. So I had to go to Boston and hear the band and everything and then we brought the band back into New York and rehearsed for a couple of weeks.
Well, did she stand in front of the band?
No, I did.
Then she just --
She just would sit down like --
Like the band singer?
Right. And I used to -- I ran the whole thing. She sang whatever I called for her to sing and

I made arrangements for her and me and Dick Vance and a few others made arrangements. And we took a trip after I got the band in shape because I added on some more men, different things, enlarged the band a little bit. I had three -- instead of the regular three trumpets and two trombones I had three trombones and four trumpets and five saxes. And then we took a trip out West, Grand Terrace and all, went all the way to California and back. And this brought us back to around 1941.
Well, '42, rather. And our last job we played was in the Earl Theater in Philadelphia with Bill Robinson.
Yeah. Then I left there and came into New York and went to work at ABC.
Why don't we stop there and then we'll continue tomorrow?
Okay.
(Recording interruption.)

When I was talking before and saying I met Eli Rice in Menocwa, Wisconsin, that was 1928. And they took our band to Milwaukee. He asked me did I play the clarinet and I told him yes, but I had never played it before. So he took me to the store and bought me a metal clarinet. And I played it the way Lester Young played the clarinet, you know.
Were metal clarinets more common those days?

Well, it was something more durable, you know. But I played it in the upper register and then I played in the low register but I didn't know anything about the bridge, you know. So when I went to Milwaukee I came in contact with this fellow, Earl Keith, who I said was a marvelous clarinet and saxophone player. And so I met Eddie Inge and he was a marvelous clarinet player and he gave me my first lesson on a clarinet. Then when I took Eddie Inge's place with Bernie Young's orchestra and went to Chicago and we were working at the Savoy Ballroom in Chicago, I started to study with a man there at the North Shore Conservatory named Joe Burns. I studied clarinet with him almost a year. And that really started me off, you know, to play the clarinet. And Joe Burns taught a lot of the reed men around Chicago at the time.
So now back to where we were --
I just wanted to say one more thing about the clarinet, you know. I guess in later years a lot of reed players started on the clarinet and then went to the saxophone.
Right.
But in the early years was it true that they started more on C melody?

Well, the saxophone players started on C melody but mostly the clarinet players, most of the guys like Barney Bigard and Omar Simeon and all those clarinet players started on clarinet because the clarinet is a much more difficult instrument to learn than the saxophone. But I just did it backwards because I guess by me being an ear player the saxophone was much easier, probably. Then I forgot to mention Sidney Bechet, of course, who was one of the all great all time reed men as far as clarinet and saxophone was concerned, jazz.
When did you become aware of Bechet?

Well, at the same time that I was listening to Coleman Hawkins I was listening to Bechet, when he was playing the clarinet and soprano saxophone. And, in fact, in 1923 I learned a solo that he played called 'Wildcat Blues.' I still play it today. I have an arrangement on it and I feature it on the tenor saxophone. I used to play it on alto. The Wildcat Blues, Sidney Bechet's.

And then I used to listen -- at that time there was another clarinet player called -- soprano saxophone player, Boyd S Center, used to boy -- but I never played any solos with him. I used to listen to most all of the reed men, you know, on record. But Bechet and Hawkins are my pick at that time.
They were the ones.

And then in later years when I came to New York I studied some clarinet with Joe Allard. We became good friends and I picked up some clarinet on him. In fact, I got into a little EMBROCHURE trouble one time and I had to go to him and he straightened it out in one lesson.

And now after -- you know, we were supposed to continue on with Ella Fitzgerald. In fact, we finished this theater with Bill Robinson in Philly. They were going to take Ella from the band -- her manager wanted to take her from the band and put her with a group called the Five Keys. And then I was to continue with the band. And my oldest daughter was going to be the vocalist. And so that was the promise, you know, that was in "Down Beat" and all that.

And when the bookings -- they had some fragment bookings left for Ella on weekends. So they would have me come and get the band and do these jobs. Well, the band, knowing that the work was getting scarce, guys started getting out and getting their own work. On weekends when I had to go out over there I almost had to organize a new band every weekend, you know, and playing the music what we had. And I just got disgusted and gave up the band. And I went over to Atlantic City where my wife was working. She was working over there in the night club and Benny Carter came over. And this was about the time that Raymond Scott put his group together over to

NBC, Ben Webster and -- well, anyway, Benny asked me, Benny Carter said that they needed an alto player at NBC and would I like to do it because they wanted him to do it and he couldn't make it. And I said, fine. So I came over to New York.
Okay, before we do this, I noticed in the first edition of the encyclopedia it mentions here that you played with your own combo which we talked about. But it says you played with Coleman Hawkins.
This was later.
Oh, they have it wrong as far as the years.

I played with Coleman Hawkins -- well, I played with Coleman Hawkins -- we had a band at the Kelly's Stables. And I'm trying to figure when it was. It was somewhere in that area between the time that I was working -- at the time that I came back to New York in '38 and '41 when I took out Ella's band.
Yeah. Here it says, Ella Fitzgerald's orchestra, '40; small combos around New York City including Coleman Hawkins and own; Benny Carter, '41.
Right. That's when we were in Kelly's Stable with Hawk.
Yeah. Because I remember reading about Hawk having a band in Kelly's stables that Don Byas
played in, too.
Well, that was when he just had the two tenors.
Yeah, that was later.

They played in Kelly's Stables and also the Famous Door, too. But that was when Hawk had a rhythm section and himself and they just added Don. Because Don was such a great player, you know, he really loved Don. But this was before that. I went in Kelly's Stables with Hawk before I went into the radio station.

And the funny thing about it, Hawkins never liked to look back at things, you know. So we used to do an arrangement on -- I was only playing clarinet then, by the way, because we had Hawk and myself and I forget who was playing trumpet at that time. So we were doing -- did the St. Louis Blues. And in rehearsal Hawk said, well, we'll play it with an old ragtime feeling, a corney feeling, and everybody take a ragtime solo, you know. And when they got to his solo he just went on and played, you know. So I said, well, Hawk, why don't you play one of them oldtime Fletcher Henderson slap-tone solos that you used to play. "I never played like that. I never played anything like that." I said, okay, I'll bring you a record tomorrow. And I brought Dick DoGlyde up where he was slap-timing, you know. And he said, "no, man, that wasn't me. I don't want to hear that, you know.
He was a marvelous guy. I liked Hawk.
He liked to argue, didn't he?
I loved him. Huh?
He liked to argue for the say, you know.
Well, musically he liked to agitate a little bit, you know. He loved a good jam session and a good musical argument, you know. Where -- that was right in his --
Well, I remember once I was in his company and he was having an argument with somebody about the merits of Horowitz and Reubenstein and he was a Reubenstein man.

Yeah, he loved all of that. Anything musical, you know, he loved to get into that, playing in different keys, you know. He was very up on his instrument and his music, you know. And he was a good reader, he was a writer, he was a pianist. And he was really -- he wasn't underrated at all. He was the daddy. And I always recognized that. And all of the guys like Ben Webster and these guys Hawk loved like Don Byas and Ben Webster, they were all good friends. But they had their differences, you know.

But Ben had his thing he could do great. I mean, he was a great ballad player. You couldn't take that away from him. And Hawk could play everything. But Don Byas, I think, shot a little bit above both of them because he could do

everything and he had the finesse that neither Ben nor Hawk had. And I think he was really the HEIFETZ (PHONETIC) of the tenor saxophone. And anyway they all were great and I respected them all very much. And I have tapes on all of them. I have about 15 hours of Hawk, I have about 10 hours of Don Byas, I have about five or six hours of Ben. And there's a new album out I'm getting ready to get now that is just exported in. In fact, Ben and I were like brothers because his grandmother used to have a restaurant in Kansas City and she used to feed Ben and I, you know. And we were always hanging out together and running around together then. So whenever we got ready to eat we'd go to his grandmother's restaurant and eat and it didn't cost us anything.

She used to make pies and I loved strawberry pie. And she used to make me a whole pie. And I would get a quart of milk and sit there and eat it and wouldn't give Ben any of it. And he never would forget it. Years later he always said, he called me Bull and I named him Frog. And he would say, she made Bull a whole pie. He never did forget that.

Then when he was -- you know, we always came together. I have letters from him now, you know, from when he first went to Europe. And he was telling me how he and Don USED TO PLAY billiards AND HOW. in Holland. He was trying to beat Don at the billard table but Don was a little bit too much for him. But they fell out somewhere along the line because when I went to Europe, which I'll come to later, they were both there and they weren't

very friendly with each other.
But where was I now?
Getting ready to go in the studio.

Yeah. So anyway, I came over to see about the job. And I went -- he told me to go see John Hammond. So I went to see John and John said, well, you're a little bit too late because Raymond has already gotten George Johnson. That's the guy --
Yeah, that's the guy who pulled in front of you in the old Ford.
Yeah. But he said, ABC, you know WJC and ABC were the -- what was that station?
WJZ?
Yeah, they were combined then, WJZ and ABC were in one station.
WJZ was the American Broadcasting Company. There was WEAF. There was the Red Network and the Blue Network.
All right. So he said, I think they're going to put some colored on. This was the beginning of this thing. And I'll call you.

So anyway, a couple of weeks later I get a telegram from John Hammond that he's sending me and Earl Bostick and Jerry Blake (PHONETIC) over to the broadcasting company to make an audition for the job because they're going to hire

some blacks on the thing. So anyway, I got the job. And I went in on tenor. I wanted to play tenor and I went in on tenor. And this was the first -- I was the first black to be on the staff. I mean, they had Raymond -- Raymond Scott had Ben and George, but that wasn't a staff job. And I was on the staff and I was the first black to be on the staff in a radio station. And that was on the Blue Network.

And on that network I played with the guys like -- the conductors, the first fellow was Joe Rines, if you remember. Joe Rines, I made audition for him and we had Sid Stoneberg, Salton Seller (PHONETIC) and Louis Martin on alto, Sid Stone was the lead alto and then Salton Seller was playing clarinet and tenor and then I was on the other tenor.

Well, I remember definitely when we made the audition. And they had us to go up to the mike and play and sit down, play blending and all that. So now later on I was told by Sid Stoneberg that the whole reed section was on notice until I came in there. And when I came in they cancelled all the notices.

So I was over there on that staff for four years. And the conductors were like Joe Rines and Paul Levalle (PHONETIC) that did "Lower Basin Street" with Paul Levalle. Nathan Van Cleave (PHONETIC), Bernard Green, Joe Stokepack. And I did the Don McNeil's Breakfast Show whenever it came there, under the direction of Eddie Balentine. And then when Paul Mike Whiteman
came up there as the president, he was conducting the Connie Boswell Show and I was in that orchestra, too.

Then in the meantime in the radio station you had other opportunities to play other places. And I played, you know, with every -- all of the sessions and things that were around. Then I did some work with -- I played with Red Allen. I was with Red Allen quite a bit. We played Max Kamansky and Bobby Hackett. And meanwhile Coleman Hawkins and Wilbur deParis and Louis Armstrong. And the Dukes of Dixieland, Roy Eldridge --
This is all during '42 to '46?

No, this is during that time after, see. And the Dukes of Dixieland, Roy Eldridge, Lionel Hampton, and then I did a record for Chaney Scott, did the thing called the Billie Holiday Story. They didn't release that because the Billie Holiday Foundation or whatever it was put a suit in and the record wasn't released. But he was in there.
When was this made?
Oh, heck, this was done around 1960 or so.

Oh, after her death, yeah. But the girl that sang it was named Chaney Scott. And I did records, you know, with Larry Darnell and Harry Belafonte and Nat King Cole, Billy Daniels, Andy Williams and Charlie Chavers. In fact, I was at the Metropole with Charlie Chavers when the

Metropole was running big.
So now while I was on the staff I decided to go back
to school. And I went to Rhodes School (PHONETIC) and got my
high school diploma. And really I did that because I was
studying the Schillinger system with Tom Timothy and so one
day I walked out and ran into Rodriguez --
: Tito (PHONETIC)?
The piano player.
: You mean Ron Ramirez?
No, Rodriguez.

: I don't know. The only Rodriguez
I know is Tito.

This is not Tito. I can't think.
Well anyway, I'll probably think of it. And Rodriguez says,
'Why don't you come and start in the Juilliard'
I'm going to start in the Juilliard. I said, I don't want
to start in the Juilliard because, I mean, I don't need that
academic.' He said, 'man, come on go with me.' So I went with
him up to Juilliard and I got interested. But I didn't have
any money so he paid my downpayment on my tuition. So I started
into Juilliard. And at the time I was going to Juilliard Miles
Davis was going there and all that.
Anyway, I was --
: This is about '45?
No, not that late. About --
: '44, then. Because Miles wasn't there

No, he wasn't there long. But I think it was about '43. I think. But anyway, I started going there and then my friend Dick Vance, he started to go there the same time that I did, the year after I went. But while I was studying in Juilliard I was studying the Schillinger (PHONETIC) system and I was pretty well along with it. So my teacher at Juilliard was studying the Schillinger System from me on Saturday. And the funny thing about it, from my experience everytime he got up in class and gave a theory he would always apologize, "of course we have a man in the class here that knows this can be done otherwise," and all like that.

But anyway, I was majoring in composition in Juilliard and it worked out pretty good. I went there about two years. Then I stopped because it wasn't nothing -- but I did graduate from Rhodes High School. And I opened my own studio right on 48th Street over Manny's and started teaching. Well, my teacher, Tom Timothy, was sending me his overflow from his class.
Teaching saxophone or --

I was teaching clarinet and composition. And I had some good students like Bill Verplank (PHONETIC), he started with me. And several others. The fellow that died, his brother's a saxophone player here now. He studied with me. What was the saxophone player, the red fellow, that
Oh, Walt Lavinsky?

Yeah, well, his brother Kermit Lavinsky. He studied with me and he was a fine tenor player. But he studied composition with me and he finally ended up in Hollywood writing for movies and pictures and everything. But he committed suicide a few years ago.

Then I had a lot of pupils. I was doing very good teaching and then I was working on the staff, too. Then finally Hank D'Amico and Vernon Brown and Billy Butterfield and a bunch of them came over on the staff and they all were playing with Paul Lavalle so I was playing with them. Then finally they gave Hank a band and I was the arranger. And I wrote a lot of things for that station while I was up there.

And then finally -- Hallwood said they hired me at that time because of the war, you know, and they wanted to make it look good that they had -- I was the only Negro in there, you know. They wanted to make it look good. So when the war was over, 1946 it was when I got my notice with 25 other men -- got their notice. And everybody was eventually hired back but me. And "Down Beat" had it in the paper, they said, well, with Barefield's seniority he should fight this. And I got a lot of calls to take up -- go back and fight the case.
And I was busy. I went from there to WOR with Cy Oliver doing the Dorsey Show. And that was good. And then
Endorsed by
after I did the Dorsey Show with Cy we -- Cy and I got together to organize that band he had. He didn't know any musicians because he had just come out of Tommy Dorsey's band so he --
That's when you went to the Zanzibar?

That's right. So I helped him organize that band, which was supposed to be between the two of us but it didn't work out that way. Anyway, I'm the one that got George Dorsey in the band on first, then we had George Dorsey and I was playing clarinet third, and had Willard Brown on baritone and let's see, who were the tenor players? I can't remember now who was playing tenor.

I want to backtrack a little bit. You know, you mentioned Miles Davis at Juilliard. I remember the first time I heard Miles Davis was Symphony # Sid introduced one of those fraternal clubhouse sessions. And this was 1945 and I never got the name. I didn't find out until much later who it was because he said, "that little student from Juilliard," you know. And it was Miles and he was kind of sputtering away in the back when everybody was on stage for the finale.

But the first time I heard you was at one of these sessions. I think it was at Lincoln Square. Not Fraternal Clubhouse, but this was the time when there used to be, every Sunday afternoon, one of the other places there was a session, you know. And that whole period was so rich as far as I'm
concerned, you know, in musicians working in New York. Because 52nd Street was going and you had all the players who were, you know, getting into the so-called be-bop.
Everybody was right in that area then, too, you know.
Yeah, and you had the musicians who had been established a while and you had the younger be-bop musicians and you had a blending.
Royal Roof.
NO, this was before the Royal Roofs.
Was it?
Yeah. This was still just when the street was going. And you would have, you know, Don Byas and Hawk playing with Dizzy's band. Had Milt Jackson, had Ray Brown.
Yeah. Well, I was on the staff at that time.
Yeah, you were making the sessions.

Because I used to come over to the street after I got off from work. Because we didn't work after say 9:00 o'clock. We were finished at the station and I did all the sustaining work over there, you know. So that --
I was going to ask you because remember that night I met you when you were playing with Brooks? We were talking about Bird. What did you think when you heard
Bird? Or had you heard him when he was first starting out?

The first time when Bird came out, you know, I was in Kansas City when he first came out to play. He sounded so bad that we wouldn't let him play. And he went down to Oklahoma and stayed about six months with Fletcher Smith who really taught him a lot about his playing. And he came back and just washed everybody out.

The only thing about Bird that didn't really knock me out, and I don't want to take anything away from him because I think the man was a genius and he was -- had an extraordinary musical mind. But his sound, you see, it wasn't a standard sound. Although it fit what he did. Because he couldn't play the first chair no place. Well, he didn't read that well in the first place.

But you have to have a knowledge of chord structures and a knowledge of the 12 tones that you're working with instead of just going ahead haphazardly and doing it. You can't do it by ear. You take all of the guys like Dizzy and Charlie Parker and they weren't playing by ear like we played. See, they sat down and worked out tools to play so they had these things, have them at their hands. If you listen to their solos you'll hear it. You build up a vocabulary of words. This is the way the jazz players play today but with a vocabulary of harmonic tools to play. Monk always would try to play like Art Tatum and he just didn't have the technique to do it. But he had a marvelous music sense. He found out that he could play any note and harmonize it with any chord and he started playing that thing which is only a rhythmic pattern (Humming). And he would play chords against it and everything. And that's where the be-bop came in.

And Dizzy had the knowledge. So he started going into Stravinsky and all these things, finding out how to split the octave, you know. That's what using the flatted fifth is, splitting the octave, see. Because you have six semitones from C to F sharp and six semitones back to C. That's what you call splitting the octave. So they could go farther than that

but [they didn't]. That's as far as they went.
So then they would take and expand the scale, see.
Expand the scale, instead of playing C, D, E, G, they expand
the scale into thirds. That makes you have C, E, G, and flat
the seventh which makes a dominant sound, C,E,G,B flat, D.
And then F, you can use the F natural but make the F sharp
and then you go to A. Then you've got the whole 11th chord
with the 13th added on top. Then next they would be back to
C. So they used this whole thing instead of using the triad
or seventh chord or ninth chord, they extended it out to use
the 11th. That's why they call it -- it's really the fourth
step of the scale but when you count from C, an octave above,
it's an 11th. And they raised it and called it the 11th
sharp. Then they take that same 11# sharp and change it to
a five flat and put it in bass. Then you have -- you're
altering a dominant chord so it will move a half step down
to the next cycle of the 5th.
And they went through all this -- well, Stravinsky
was doing these things and it just transferred over to jazz.
And that's how they worked it. And when you hear guys play

And so he called me and said, look, he said. 'You did me a great favor,' he says. 'I'm going to make you rich.' He says, 'All you got to do now, stick with me,' and this guy never went to bed. He was book -- he was really wild, and then he was renovating this building, had a building next door and had big display windows of fur coats and manniquins and everything where he was going to put this show in.
And he dropped dead.
(Laughter.)
And --
How old a man was he?

About 40, 39 years old. He had Berger's disease. And he always -- he kept on, and he says -- I was, you know, he'd seen me exercising, and he says, soon as we get this show straight, I'm going to get with you and you can show me some exercises and all that. Of course, he limped on one foot. And he dropped dead.

So anyway, after he dropped dead, well, all the people that he had gotten money from started grabbing the show, and the show stayed in Miami, I imagine, about two, three months and then we went to Vegas and stayed out there three months. And then we came back to Washington -- and we came back to Washington, and we came back to New York and did Central Park, and then that was-- and then the show broke up.

But if Murray Wanger hadn't died, I think that thing would have been one of the big things, and I think, as he said, he would have made me rich because, you know, in fact, when the payday come, they paid all the band off. And they came -- and the manager, they came and gave me a check like the band, and I wouldn't accept it because -- so I go back and see him.
And he says, well, look, here's a check. He says, just write in your price, what you want on it.
(Laughter.)

And I wrote in double what the other guys were getting. But anyway, now, I made about three, $4,000.00 for the music that I had written, you know, but this was one quirk of life, things, the way things happen.
When did you go to Europe with Sammy Price?
Now, this was before --
This was after the --
After the show.

This was after the show, because we went to Europe in '58 with Sam, and then we came back and took another show -- another show down in Miami that year, in '58 too, which didn't last very long, with Cab Calloway.
Now, you were -- was this the first time you went to Europe?
No, I was in Europe with Cab in 1934.

Yeah, all right. But you were going to tell me something about -- you mentioned something about your meeting somebody over there or something before you mentioned when we were talking. Was that with Sammy Price?
No, this was another time.
Oh, this was later, right.
But anyway, when -- I went to

Europe with Sammy, that was the year the Pope died. We went over -- it was Doc Cheetam and Sammy and J. C. Higginbotham, and we took another trumpet player to take -- Elmer Crumley took two trombones in case Hickey didn't, because at that time Hickey had the biggest name of everybody. So he -- the job was booked on the strength of Higginbotham, but to play safe we took Elmer Crumley along as an extra trombone in case Hickey got, you know, juiced or anything.

And we had J. C. Heard on drums and Sammy and Lewis on bass, Jimmy Lewis on bass. And we took a girl, and I don't remember her name, a singer. Anyway, she stayed over there. We went over to Paris. We went over on -- we took the boat over, went on, over on the Mary, Queen Mary, one of these -- and we went to Paris, and we stayed around Paris about a week.
We played -- that was at the Columbia -- called the Columbia --
Olympia?

Olympia. And then we went on down to Holland, and we stayed -- oh, they had everything set up for us, and then when the Pope died, the whole trip was cancelled. And the rest of the fellows went back to Paris to wait for the boat, and I took a plane from Holland, Amsterdam, come on back to New York. By the time they got back here, I was working, you know.
And then they got another show that fall to go to

Miami for Cab, another Cotton Club show. Some other guys got an idea to put on a Cotton Club show like they did before because that one was such a hit, but it didn't last too long, although they were still using Benny Davis and the music.

And now in '59 they put a show together for Cab which he didn't know nothing about to go to South America, but I was the music director. And Cab calls me. He says, what is this show about? I said -- I tell him, well, it's going to be a pretty good show. So we'll have him, Leslie Scott and a lady named -- blues singer named Washington, had chorus girls and they had -- it was put together by a man named Valdez, and we were going down to the Copacabana in Rio de Janeiro.

So we got the show together, and we went down, and when we get there, we had the -- we didn't take a band. I only took a drummer, and we used the musicians down there. And we played in Rio for -- we were in Rio for about three or four weeks. Then we went to this -- not San Paolo. We did go to San Paolo. But we went to Santos. We went to Bel Rizante -- this is all in Brazil, and we -- I think in -- Bel Rizante was where they was having a revolution there, and we didn't finish the show because they turned the lights out on us, and we had to come out.
Then we want to São Paulo, and we played there, and then we went to Argentina, went down to Buenos Aires, and we played in Buenos Aires and landed up in Montevideo, and then we
come on back to -- came back to New York. We went to San Paolo and caught a plane and came back. We were down there about eight weeks. It was a nice trip.
And then after we came back from there, then the next year, 1960, I took the show to Europe calle the Jazz Train.
I was going to ask you about that. MR. : Yeah, and that's (inaudible).
What was that?

That was a show made up from -- well, it was -- Jazz Train was the history, supposed to be a history of American jazz with theater, and we did things like Porgy and Bess and -- and it was a nice show. We had Leslie Scott. He was the star. And Ura Lee Unitas -- I forgot her -- she was, you know, a singer, a great fine (inaudible) singer. And we had Cooken Brown and had a chorus line. And we had about 40 people.
And we went to -- went from here to Rome. We opened in Rome for a week, and we didn't take -- I took a drummer, only had a drummer and had to use Italian musicians.
Who was the drummer?
Tommy Benford. And we went to -- went to -- from there down -- we went to about 15 cities in Italy, and one of the main places was Milano. We stayed there quite a bit.
Now, you were the conductor or did
I just conducted.
You didn't play at all.
I took -- I wrote myself into the overture. That's the only thing I did. And at least to get something playing, I wrote my clarinet into the overture. I was playing mostly just clarinet.

And we went to -- we played -- we ended -- after we played all over Italy, and then we went from Italy to Germany, we played in Munich and Berlin, a week in each place and then went down to, went to, oh, can't think of the place. Well, we went to two, three places in Germany, and we ended up in Switzerland. We went up there in Switzerland.

When we got in Switzerland, they offered business -- at least they say the business wasn't too good, so they wanted everybody to work on percentage. So I -- that's when I left there. I came back to New York.

Now, then when I got back to New York, what's this -- oh, I came back to New York, and I became an actor, and I did the play, Angel in the Pawn Shop with -- in fact, I was the original Angel in the Pawn Shop opened on Broadway right after I finished Streetcar Named Desire, and I made a reading for it, and they didn't hire me because I was bald-headed. It was just -- the story was about a clarinet player that came into a pawn shop to pawn his clarinet under the condition that the

pawn shop owner would let him come and practice every day, and it finally ended up where he was in there practicing -- the girl there talked the pawn shop broker into letting him do this. And at the end of the picture some robbers came in and robbed the pawn shop, and the clarinet player conked them on the head with the clarinet, you know.

But it was a pretty good show. Anyway, I was -- I didn't get the original show. Willie Lewis got it. Remember Willie Lewis? Clarinet player -- well, he got it, and he was almost as bald as I, but he wasn't the clarinet player that I was, you know, but he got it.

And so when they had the -- in 1960, they didn't hired me because I was bald -- so now in 1960 when they got ready to do this Angel in the Pawn Shop in summer stock in Philly at the Theater In the Round, they called me, and I did it, and I was the only one that got raving notices, you know.

And I say, I was up on the clarinet. I could play cadenzas and things, just a few cadenzas here that you had to play and you had to do some lines. And then that next year in 1961 they organized another Cotton Club show in the Winter Garden on Broadway, and I was the conductor for that. And then we piled after that -- oh, I'm trying to think of the fellow that wrote the music for that. I knew him very well, but he hasn't been around. He's in California somewhere. Can't even think of the tune, one of the tunes he wrote too.

But anyway we moved that Cotton Club from -- this Cotton Club on Broadway was padlocked or something, and we finally moved it out to Golden Slipper on Long Island, in -- oh, I forget the place out there.
Then you got involved with --
That was 1962.
Well, you know, what about the playing with Paul Laval, the Freedom --

Well, this comes next, 1963. I got a call that Paul Laval wanted a tenor player. Paul called me because I had worked with him in radio. We had become good friends, and he called me to come up and work with him at Freedom Land on tenor, so I bought a tenor. I didn't have one at the time.

And I bought the tenor, which I'm still playing, and went to Freedom Land. Now, during the time at Freedom Land Paul was telling me that the World Fair was coming in, and the next year after I was there, and he wanted a drummer. So the drummer that I took to South America with me, Sol Hall, I put him in touch with Sol. And Sol went out to the World Fair.
Well, the first year of the World Fair I didn't go. I had something else to do. That was '64, I think, and I did some shows. I was doing -- I did the marathon 33 with June Havoc.
Oh, yeah, I saw that.
And the trombone player -- he's acting now.
I don't know why I remember what's his name for that show, Higgie Wolfrington.
Yeah, but the trombone player, Conrad Janis.
Conrad Janis.
Yeah, he had the band.
Yeah.

So Panama Francis was in that and this boy, Pretty Eddie, the drummer, he was Panama's understudy there. We did -- then we did another show with Dennis O'Keefe called 'Never Sleep Over a Pretzel Factory' right after that, then Max the Mirror or Max Cavulli had a place out in Brooklyn, and we used to play -- called Max the Mirror -- we used to play out there.

And then there was another job, Snaghead's Inn, and we -- I did some records with Dick Vance and Benny Morton on my own, you know, with the -- and then there was a play -- I was with a guy yesterday called Awfully Nice that I conducted. We went up to New Haven and up to Philly. It didn't go very far.
Yeah. And then you played with Walter de Paris.
Frank -- with Frank Stewart. And
then there -- then there was the Broken Drum, where I played with Wilbur de Paris. But I played with Wilbur de Paris also down to Jimmy Ryan's too, you know.
Uh-huh. I guess he was the last band to play at the old Jimmy Ryan's.
Yeah.
Before they tore it down.

And then 1965 was -- I was freelancing most of that time. We went in the Riverboat Room -- and then 1966 with -- oh, I did some things at the City Center, some musicals at the City, you know, the City Center, and then I was at the Riverboat with Cab Calloway, and then I was at the Riverboat again with Cab and Cab with Ella Fitzgerald and Earl Hines, me and Bud Johnson and a little boy named Don something, saxophone player.
1967 I went to Canada with Willie Lion Smith. In fact, Willie --
Was that the first time you had been associated with Willie?
No, I've been --
Since the Streetcar --
Yeah, well, I've known him, but this is the first time since then. But Willie and Don Ewell made an album, and so they went into the Colony up in --
Toronto.

-- Toronto. And the guy -- I forgot the guy that booked it, but he got an idea that it would be nice for them to have a horn, so they sent for me, and I went up to play. An alto and clarinet and two pianos, no drum, no rhythm section at all. We stayed there three weeks, and it was very nice. And -- but only thing, Don Ewell had a harder -- almost had a stroke, and he had to go in the hospital opening night, opening night.
And the second night and we sent and got Claude Hopkinson. He came up and finished the job. So the three of us did that job. And --
And then, of course, you started going to Europe, and you started touring.
Well, I went to Canada again in '68.
Well, what about the Jazz Giants in '67? What was that about?
I don't remember that, Jazz Giants, unless you're talking about the Saints and the Sinners.
No, that comes later.
Well, the only --
Here it says, played in Jazz Giants with own band '67, toured (inaudible) in Africa summer '69, with Saints and Sinners in Europe late in --
Well, the Jazz Giants --
Was that a tour or what?
-- that would have been --
That quite a bit --
That might have been Red Holland and the -- because that's what he called his gang, the Jazz Giants.
Did you go on a tour with him?

Well, we played -- Red and I played all around, out in Brooklyn and all around this area together. And in fact when Red took sick, I took his place down in Blues Alley when he was down in Washington and then I went back there for Tom Gwaltney about three weeks a couple of times a year until Tom sold the place to somebody else.

But in '68 then I went back to play with Don Ewell at the Golden Nugget in Toronto, and then -- and then I started going to the Poconos -- and then we had a group that taught school for -- out in Pratt University for the summer, for the summer session, and I think --
In Brooklyn?

Yeah, we had a summer class out there. That was during the days when they were, what was it called, keeping down the hot summer with the riots and stuff, and they -- we went out there to teach. They practically donated a building to us.
Oh, yeah, that was during Lindsay's administration.
Yeah, and they donated -- they

donated a building for -- and they had about ten of us, Joe Bill Newman, Norris Turner and me and Heywood Henry and a bunch of us went out there and was teaching underprivileged children out there, but that did -- that only lasted one summer.

And then I went -- in '68 also I went to Ali Baba for 18 weeks of my own trio, you know, on 59th Street. And I had -- that was nice. I enjoyed that. I had a drummer, what was it? Skippy White on drums and the piano player that was with me for a while, and I had Sonny White playing piano.

And then in '69 I went to Toronto again. That was when I went -- I took my own band up to Toronto with Dick Vance and Jimmy Crawford and Benny Morton, and I think Sonny White went up there with me. And then I went to Africa.
Yeah, now, what was that? What kind of a band did you take there?

Well, when I went to Africa, I went to Africa with -- it was Dick Vance's group. And we went -- we had four pieces, and we went there to play the American Dance Theater. We had Avon Long and Cookan Brown and Gib Gibson and the Park Dancers, you know, Mrs. Park.
Rosa Park -- not Rosa -- Mama Lou Parks.
Mama Lou Parks and her dancers. And we played nine countries and 22 cities in Africa. We went to Nigeria. We went to Ethiopia. We went to Morocco, Tunisia
and Guinea, Ghana, Senegal. We went all over.
You went all over.
And they made a documentary of it in the State Department.
(Side B.)
What I meant by documentary, you know, they made movies of the whole trip, and I think Dick Vance has some of the movies. They were not available to everybody, but he has them.
And after coming back from Africa I -- that next year I took a trip, in 1969 I took a trip with Red Richards, Saints and Sinners, back to Europe again, and we had Buddy Tate and Herman Autrey.
Yeah, I remember reading about that.

And Red and the drummer -- I can't think of -- Reed, George Reed on drums and -- the fellow we called The Fox, the white fellow, bass player, he's from Pittsburgh. I don't remember his name anyway. And we all -- and we had -- we went to France and played mostly all through France.
You were playing clarinet at this time?
Yeah. In fact, what happened, when we left here, we were supposed to open in London, but somehow with the thing, when we got to London, they didn't need us.
We didn't even get off the plane there. We went to Copenhagen to play this -- our thing for Timmy Rosenkrantz. It was a memorial to Timmy Rosenkrantz.

Well, one of the biggest -- we were only there in Copenhagen one day, but the biggest thrill -- one of the biggest thrils I had was when I walked into this hall that night. Ben Webster was standing there. And I hadn't seen Ben for maybe four or five years or five or six years. And we had such a good time talking to each other, because I'd been getting letters from him, you know. And that wasn't enough.
I went up on stage, went backstage, and who else do you think I -- was there? Don Byas. And I'd been to Europe, hadn't seen him for about 25 years or 20 years.
Well, he didn't come back here until '69.

Yeah. And I had been to Europe several times looking for him, and he was always someplace else. And this was really a great reunion to find Ben and Don there together. The only heartbreaking thing was that they weren't friendly with each other, you know, friendly with each other.
Both guys (inaudible) they weren't talking?
Well, they weren't friendly with each other, but I made them get together. In fact, and Teddy Wilson
was there and Charlie Shavers and -- in our group. And at night Teddy was playing at some -- Teddy was playing -- played one of the places there, and we all went over there that night.

So I told Don to come over and meet me over there, and I went over with Ben and some friends of his. And we went in the back part, and Ben ordered food and everything. And then Don got there, and I went in -- Don and I played with Teddy. And then after the thing was over with, we all went back in the back and sat down in the kitchen part.

And then we had to leave the next morning, so Don and I left Ben there, because Ben never went to bed until daybreak, no time anyway. So Don and I left. And I went on to my hotel, and Don went to pick up some books or something he was going to get. And then I left that next morning.

But any -- we went on, left there, and we went down to -- no, I think we played Zurich. Then we went from Zurich down to Barcelona. We flew down to Barcelona. And then after we played Barcelona, we took a bus and came all -- it was a wonderful trip. We came by bus. It was one nighters all up through France, all the way back into Paris, and then we went -- also went to Belgium.

And it was nice. It was really nice. We got to see all the countryside and everything and traveling like. Today, the way they travel today by plane, you don't get to see anything, and you spend most of your time in the airports, and
you're always staying at some place outside of the town. But when you have a bus, it's much easier to leave when you get ready and -- and stop and eat and -- it was a lot of fun.

And you get to know the people and the whole atmosphere. Well, it's the same thing here in the United States. You can be in any city if you're staying in a Holiday Inn. You could be almost anyplace. Same thing.
Yeah, it's the same thing. That's what I was really talking about.
And when you used to travel around and, you know --
We always went into the heart of the city.
The bands years ago --
Yeah.
-- each place had its own --
That's right.
-- character.

That's right. But today it's all Holiday Inn or some facsimile. And then the -- after I come back from Europe with Red, I took a trip out to see my sister in Des Moines. And then in 1970 Ty Ree Glenn Tyree Glenn was working at the Roundtable, and he took a vacation, so I went in there with the trio, with Norman Simmons and -- well, it's a quartet -- Norman Simmons and Eddie Locke and [Vic] Sproles Vic Sproles, a bass player. That was a

nice couple of weeks.
And then I went to Cleveland that same year with Red -- Richard at the Theatrical Grill. We went to -- also went to Pittsburgh. There was a place in Pittsburgh -- we played in a hotel called Basin Street. And then I went out that same year with Georgie Jessel and his show. And we played -- then I played -- we had some schools, and we were playing jazz out to a lot of the schools in Long Island, which we do some now, still do.
For what program is that? Under what --

Well, Camera de Cameron -- you ever hear of them? Well, that's the -- I can't explain it, but it's a lady that has -- she books all these schools, and you go out and play jazz with movies for the kids, you know.
Uh-huh. Who have you been doing that with?

Me, Bennie Morton and -- oh, they've changed the personnel from time to time. Earl -- oh, I know Dick Vance has done some of them on trumpet. And -- names don't come to me. It's (inaudible). But after that, then I went down to Blues Alley in '71 with Red, and then I started to working at the Poconos every summer. I worked at the Poconos every summer from '71 up until '75, through '75.
One particular place or several
places or --

At the Unity -- Unity House, yes, Unity House. And then in the spring, every spring since '71 I've been doing Ringling Brothers Circus at the Garden when they come into the Garden. And we're getting ready to start it tomorrow out in Coliseum.
Nassau?
Yeah, for the same --
This the first time you played it out at Nassau?
No, no, every year since -- every year since '71.
Both places.

Uh-huh. We do -- well, we started out doing eight weeks at the Garden, and now we're doing 12, and this year we're going to do 13 weeks at the Garden. And we do -- always do about ten days to two weeks out in Nassau every year in November. And they're coming to the garden in March.
Right.

And then I went in '72 -- also went to Canada with Earl Hines playing at the Sauveron, you know, with his group. And now -- so that's -- now, the rest of the time since '71-'73 -- '71 up until now I've been on the house band at the Garden, play the ice shows, Holiday on Ice, Ice Capades, Moscow Circus and whatever shows and the circus,
whatever comes in there. I don't know what's going to happen now because my contract died a month ago.
Oh, how did that come about? How did you get that to begin with?
Well --
Contractor?
No.
Contractor come in with you or --

There was a contractor named Charlie Cotterson that had this job at the Garden and -- with Ringling Brothers Circus. And Jones, Renauld Jones, a trumpet player, was playing in this band, and Renauld recommended me for the job on the reed section. So I went in the reed section playing baritone sax.

And then Charlie Cotterson's contract ran out, and Jack Shannon got the -- got the job. And then I started working for him doing all the show, not only just the circus, all the shows. And I was -- At the Felt Forum
(Inaudible) for him too as well as (inaudible).
(Inaudible) for him, yes, we always do the Moscow Circus in the Felt Forum, but I switched from baritone to tenor, which I really wanted to play tenor anyway, and so I got the --
: I think I saw you one night going in for the Moscow Circus.
Uh-huh.
: I was going up to the employees' entrance to the Garden for a hockey game, and you had gone in the other.
So now -- then so 1976 I went to Nice. In fact, in 1973 -- George Wein called me to put together a Chick Webb band for the Carnegie Hall with Ella.
: Right.

And we did that. And I arranged the music and did that, and then the same year I did a Cab Calloway alumnus with Cab for this same festival. And then I went to the jazz festival in Nice in '76 and '77, and I'm going this year, in '79. In fact, in '76 I went just as a tenor player. '77 I went with Cab Calloway, and this year, in '79 I'm going with Lionel Hampton.

I didn't go in '78.

Right.

Yeah, Arnett Cobb and myself.
: Uh-huh. This going to be a big
Yeah.

And then I just came back from Boston. I was up there about a month ago with Ray Bryant playing at Loulu's.
Playing tenor?
Yeah, that's all I -- I refuse --
When I heard you with Brooks Kerr at Fortune Garden, you were playing tenor.
Yes, right. I refuse to play anything else right now, unless it would be a show, a Broadway show or something like that. Tenor -- I'm having a love affair with the tenor saxophone.
I made an album last year for Famous Door.
Has it been released?
Yes, it's been released. Released a year ago -- called the Indestructible E. B. And I had me and Warren Vache and John Faddes. Panama Francis did some of
the sides, and Mosey Alexander did the other side. Milt Hinton and John Bunche -- and Bucky Pizzarelli did some of them.
What was the band you had at the Seafood Palace, that thing that didn't last too long? I know they had several different bands in there, but I know you had a band over there.
Seafood --
Yeah, where Gluckstein's used to be on 48th Street. This was about four years ago.
Seafood Palace.
Or something like that it was called. I know you had --
48th Street or 52nd Street?
No, 48th Street.
Because I was in Pier 52 with Frankie Dash and --

Seafood Palace.

48 -- where was it, on 48th Street?
48th Street between 8th and Broadway.
I don't remember.
You don't remember.
No. I was there?
Yeah, I remember seeing the ads and everything, you know. But I guess that's not proof. They might have advertised you and you weren't there. That's possible, though I seem to remember that --

(Laughter.)
That's right. I went to (inaudible) Europe with a guy that I was on played about a three hour concert with records, and half of them I didn't --

I knew my playing, but I didn't remember.

Yeah, yeah. I remember that.

Yeah, but she --
-- sing with the band.
Well, she was at that time -- she was studying singing, and she was going to sing. Her name is Delores. But she never followed it through. She finally got married and --
Gave up the profession.

-- gave up the whole thing. She -- but for a while she started to be a dancer like her mother, and she gave it up. And my other daughter, she always talks -- talked about singing, but she never sang. No. They never -- neither one of them followed the music business.
You had two daughters.
Yeah.
So they became --
Married and children.
