Seven times, seven grandchildren, and none of them got into music either. Roddy, he's in Milwaukee.

He's a television announcer in Milwaukee, and he -- he started to playing guitar and stuff. And then Donny, he was going to be a flautist, and he got into something else. They all got into something else.

And, oh, my other granddaughter, she's a policewoman in California, and she was going to -- she started playing flute and clarinet, and she had a beautiful voice, good singer, and she never followed -- she got into police work and -- they're all on their other little things, you know.
In looking back over your career, all the people you've known and played with, you know, what are some of the things that stand out in your mind, some of the people you've known?

Well, being like I am, I'm always -- I'm a guy that thinks a lot and reminisce a lot -- the whole, everybody, I mean, I could -- I mean, it's been just like I have a million friends, and they're all scattered every place, all in really music business, and I've been close friends to everybody from the singers like Virginia Rustian and on down. I mean anybody you name, it seems funny, and it seems funny for a person to say that they've been contacted with most everybody, but I have. I've played with and worked and been close to mostly every musician and every entertainer and singer that has ever amounted to anything.
That goes for Nat King Cole. I remember when he was

-- came to California, and I had my band out there, and he, you know, came out there with a show. And he wasn't doing anything, you know. In fact, I remember when he organized his first group. He never sang at all. He was a great piano player, fine pianist.

And we worked together out there in California, and when I come back, first thing I know, he had a trio, and the next thing I know he was singing and became a big star, you know. And Billy Daniels, everybody that you could name I've been contacted in the music business somewhere along the line either writing for them or playing with them or working with them.

In fact, Cab Calloway had mostly everybody at that time that was working with us doing theaters and shows. So just about any -- that goes for Bill Robinson, goes for Lena Horne. I mean, I knew her when she was in the Cotton Club chorus, and that goes for anybody you can name in the show business. I can tell you something about, you know, my relationships with them.
When you were with Cab, Dizzy hadn't come in the band yet or --
No, when I left Cab -- see, I left Cab, as I said, around -- just about when 1935 was going to 1936.
Six, yeah, and he didn't come until
about '39.
See, Dizzy didn't come into Cab's band until way later. In fact, when I took Ella's band -- Chick died and I took Ella's band over there, and Dizzy was in that band.
Oh, RIGHT. What was he like then?
(Inaudible).

That was -- oh, Dizzy's always been the same. He's always been a guy that likes to have a lot of fun. I mean, and everybody called him Dizzy, but he's not Dizzy at all. He's really a clever man, you know, a great musician, very talented. And there's nothing really dizzy about him. I guess it's just because he acts that way, you know.

And Bird -- well, he used to come to see me all the time, you know, because he was in trouble, you know, and I was trying to help him get himself straightened up, but it's hard for a person to -- that's weak -- to get straightened out. I've had several things with different people. I have an alcoholic brother and an alcoholic daughter, and I know how hard it is for these people to break away from things.

And it's hard for a person like me to see why they can't, but I can understand it, because I've never -- oh, I remember -- I never smoked until I was 35, when I went to work at the radio station. Well, it was 32. I was about 32 years old. Then I started to smoke. Well, I smoked for about ten years. But when I got ready to quit, I remember I quit, and
then I started again, I'd quit and I'd start, and one day I just stopped and I never did it again and had -- I had overcome the craves for it, and that was it. Now it's offensive to me.
So but you have -- it's a certain point, your breaking point that you have to go through to break off from something, you know, and some people just can't do it, I imagine.
Well, a lot of --

So that was probably -- that was Bird. Charlie -- Charlie Parker wanted to break away from the things. He was in pretty bad shape. I mean he -- but he just -- in fact, one time he showed me where he had bitten off half of his tongue, had one of those seizures or something and just bit one half of his tongue off from the middle on down to the side.

And Tyree Glen, remember -- I remember when he first came to California. I was putting -- organizing my band, and one night I was sitting up writing music, and a knock came on the door and it was Tyree Glen. He said, Mr. Barefield, I hear that you're putting together a band. I'm a trombone player. And he was a godsend because there's no trombone players out there at the time. He came right in time to play the first chair, the trombone in my band out there.
Where had he come from, then?
I don't know, because he had been around -- from around Washington, D. C., something like that, but I don't know how it happened he just come out, how he happened to get to California.
What about Fletcher? You knew him, I guess, over the years from just traveling and --

Well, I knew him, knew of Fletcher, but I really met him when I joined the band in California. And Fletcher Henderson was one of the nicest men you ever met. He was a very passive type of a person and very quiet. I remember when I -- this is really where I got together on my clarinet, in Fletcher's band, because when I went in Fletcher's band I had to play Buster Bailey's book. And the first week I quit. It was so -- the clarinet things were in such crazy keys and were so fast, and when I'd get up and play, I'd mess it up, and Fletcher would roll. He'd just fall out laughing on the piano, you know.

He sat near the piano, and he'd laugh and call it again. And I would play and mess it up, and he would -- and so I told him at the end of the first week, I said, 'Look, I am putting in my two weeks' notice.'

He says, 'What's the matter?' I says, 'I can't -- I'm not a clarinet player. I can't play these things. I mean, it's too big of a job.' He says, 'Aw, keep -- you're doing all right. Go ahead and keep trying.' So I started taking the book home.

And after the -- after a week I began to play them, and he -- (inaudible) -- and so that's why finally I started to like the clarinet and became a clarinet player, really. I had played the clarinet with Cab, but not like in Fletcher's band, taking that seat, because Hilton Jefferson was playing first and I was playing third and playing the clarinet chair, and I really developed to play clarinet.
But Smack he was a marvelous person, marvelous.
And you played with him at Cafe Society?
Yeah, that was when we had the small group, and he didn't have the music for it, but I had a book, and he used that.

Well, you know, they always talk about how, you know, he -- his band never really got the acclaim that it should have gotten, and then of course, at first, when he wrote for Benny Goodman, Benny Goodman's band got --

Right. Yeah, because he -- all of the things that he recorded in the '20s, Benny Goodman came back and got famous on them in the '30s. Don Redmon was another great musician. In fact, I worked with him -- what year? Oh, even after I recorded with him in -- in the late '30s or first of the '40s, whatever it was, I came back with him again, with Pearl Bailey, when he was conducting for Pearl Bailey. I forget what year -- years those were.
Before he died -- and --
This was the late '50s, wasn't it?

Something like that. And we played -- he had a band, a nice, a marvelous band with Pearl Bailey and Louie Belson on drums, and he had Sam Taylor and me and Sammy Most and George Dorsey, and we played around. But Don was a very unsung hero of music. I think he was one of the greatest, you know, all around musicians because he could play any instrument in the orchestra, you know. He played -- and when he was with the Cottonpickers, whoever was missing, he would just sit down and play the book, trumpet, trombone, piano, guitar; anything that he had to play, he played.
Well, he has been given credit for being, you know, really shaping the whole idea of the big band arrangement.
Right. That's right, uh-huh. And I think he's the one that really got the Mills Brothers off on the right track.
How do you mean?
Well, before Don Redmon, before they started to sing with Don Redmon, remember when Don Redmon had that commercial, radio show years -- around 1933-34?
Yeah.
Well, he had a big band and had a radio commercial. I don't know whether it was Camel cigarettes

or somebody, and he had the Mills Brothers with him. Before they met Don, they were singing wrong harmonies and everything, and after that they really got their ideas straightened out by just being, working with Don and happening to -- but it's a shame that, when he died, he didn't -- they didn't even mention his name in the funeral.
They had his funeral over on 72nd at Walter B. Cookman. The place was too small for the people in the first place, and he was a Jehovah's Witness.
Don was?
And they didn't -- they just talked about our dear brother and that was all. They didn't mention none of his accomplishments or anything.

As a reed player, of course, you played with and heard all the great reed players from an era when there were so many, and we were talking before about how each one was a great individual even if he was working in a style. Of course, Hawkins was the man who really brought the tenor saxophone out front, and people were influenced by him. But they -- but all of them had their own --

Well, as they tell you, you know, the only thing about copying, you can't copy individuality. The two -- everyone has played or were inspired to play like someone, and I think that everybody that played an instrument copied someone. But not -- but the same thing didn't come out

eventually because there's a certain individual thing that God gave everybody that's different from everybody else. And you can't -- you just can't copy it. You can get the idea, but you can't -- you can always tell the difference between the real thing and something else, and the other thing always develops into another complete style or another complete character.
You were mentioning about Ben Webster and Don Byas and --
Well, they're all --
-- Herschel Evans came out of Hawkins too, didn't he?

That's right, Herschel Evans, Don -- Lucky Thompson, Don Byas, Ben Webster, Lockjaw Davis. All of those were -- Hawk inspired players -- Ike Quebec. And then you turn around on the other hand and you'll find guys like Bud Johnson, Stan Getz, Zoot Simms and all of them were -- Zoot was half in between.
Well, he liked Ben too. He always said that.
Well, he -- Zoot is between them, but all of these things are -- developed into another character altogether.
What do you think about the whole idea of -- they're always talking about the Texas tenors.
No such thing.
And yet those guys had a certain thing where Herschel Evans, of course, came from Hawk, but he had his own --
Everybody did.
And then it seemed like guys like Buddy Tate and Jaquet and that kind of came from Herschel.
Buddy copied Herschel, because Buddy took Herschel's place in Basie's band. And Illinois Jaquet has got a lot of Lester Young in him.
Right.

You know, a little rougher, you know, and Bud Johnson is rougher, but he's -- I'll tell you a story of Illinois Jaquet and Bud. We were in Nice in 1976, and we stayed at the Meridian Hotel, and every night they had a jam session all night long, and everybody congregated there. It was a beautiful year.

And after that we'd mostly go up and hang out in Bud's room, Dizzy and Illinois and myself and Jackson, Oliver Jackson, all go up to Bud's room. You know, I never drank -- I wasn't drinking but joined the rest of them and watch them drink and tell tales.
So one night we were sitting up there in this -- in Bud's room talking and everything, and a knock came on the door. And I opened the door and here, Illinois walks in, let
the king in. Let the king --
(Laughter.)

And Bud jumped up and said, 'the king of what?' He says, 'the king, the king tenor player.' Bud says, 'Look, man. Go get your horn. I'll show you who's the king.' So they're talking. So finally they made up a pact, said, 'tomorrow night we'll meet downstairs, and I'll show you the king. Bring your horn down.'

So Bud said I'm -- Bud and Illinois are going to battle it out, so I said, 'Well, I'll bring mine down too, and we'll just all have a good time.' So that next night here comes -- Bud was down, and here comes Illinois with a soprano, drunk as he could be with a soprano saxophone.
A soprano, I never heard of him play Bud with the soprano.

That's what he had, you know, because, you know, he was asking for trouble, you know, because he's going to cut Bud, and Bud is pretty rough, you know, and I was going to get in it just for the fun of it, because I'm a new tenor player, and I relish this kind of thing anyway, you know.
So Bud said, 'The king of what?' Well, that's what he calls himself, the king.
Uh-huh. Well, he had that number with Basie. But, you know, it's --

Oh, and I tell you another thing what happened. You know, Illinois is a quiet man until he has a few drinks. So when I first got into Nice that night, we had the night off. And I come down. Here comes Illinois and Joe Newman downstairs, and they were both juiced. So they went in the restaurant, come in the restaurant and was arguing with the man because, you know, you can't get something to eat in there. And they was arguing with the man about getting something to eat.

And so I was hungry too, so I says, well, let's all of us go and find someplace to eat. So we -- Illinois and Newman and myself, we go up the street where the restaurants were, and we saw Doc Cheatham in a restaurant eating, so we went in there to sit down to eat.

And pretty soon here comes a girl with a camera, going to take pictures, you know. She said, you want a picture? I said, no picture. And Joe said no. But Illinois says, 'No, yeah, get my picture. This is an occasion. We got Moonglow Barefield over there and -- what's that thing flying -- Flying Home Jaquet and Newman, he said. So this is an occasion. Take the picture.

So the girl snapped the picture. We tried to get him not to, but she snapped the picture, and he didn't have any francs. So he give her a $20.00 bill, and I think she brought him back about $10.00 in change. And so we told him, said,

now, and she only gave him one picture.
So now, we had our dinner. He says, don't worry, fellows. I just paid for the whole dinner. I paid for everything. We said, you didn't pay for anything but the picture. So now, come to find out neither one of them had any francs. I was the only one had any francs, and I ended up paying the whole tab.
(Laughter.)

So later on Joe Newman did give me back, but Illinois -- so every time I see Joe now, I say, where's Illinois? I don't know where he is, because he -- you know, he's wild (inaudible) when he gets -- but I knew him, when I first met him, he was a tap dancer.
He was a tap dancer?
Yeah.
Where was this?

Down in Fort Worth, Texas, when I went to -- went down -- I was playing with Cab there, and we played an amateur night, you know, in Fort Worth, and Illinois was tap dancing, and they had a team called Ropo, Nopo and Shobo, and one guy was -- and they would put on a boxing thing, and the other third guy was a referee, and they did this all to music and they tap danced, an amateur contest.
(Laughter.)
word always played at at Sounds like a great routine
Somebody (inaudible). And he hadn't
taken up --
No, he might have been -- been studying the saxophone with him (inaudible), but he was just --
I have to ask him about that next time I see him.
Ask him. Ask him.
(Interruption.)
Yeah, Piney Brown ran a nightclub there called the Subway down on 18th and Vine.
Yeah, you were telling me how Piney Brown was the patron saint.

Yeah, and, you know, when all of the bands came into Kansas City, they would all collect the, you know, whatever musicians were around -- well, I used to go to the -- Ben Webster and I and Basie, we used to go down to the Subway almost every night and jam, you know.

And, well, we had Andy Kirk's band there and had Thamon Hayes' band and Bennie Moten's band, George Lee's band, and then the other bands used to come in and out. And you could be -- I could, you know, like if I'd be home asleep at 3:00, 4:00 o'clock in the morning, sometimes the phone would ring, and they say, 'Oh, man, such and such a guys are down here blowing. Get your horn and come down.'
I jumped up and put my clothes on, take my horn and go on down to the Subway. And my wife would -- leave my wife

right there in the bed, you know, and go right on down to the Subway and come on back the next day around 12:00 noon sometimes juiced and, you know, but that's where everybody -- anytime you went to Kansas City, that was the place to go, the Subway, and blow all night.
No matter -- I mean you wasn't working, you'd run down, and when you were working, you'd get off from work and stop at the Subway.

I guess that's what Roy Eldridge and Chu Berry are talking about on that record, of 'Sittin' In.' sitting, and he says, "Where you working?", you know, and had that little "I'm working down at the Subway." A conversation on the Subway.

Yeah. And it -- and that's everywhere you went that that happened, and we would -- we would, like we went to a town and ran into a couple of bands, and the guys would be in the hotel lobby, starting to talking about playing, and first thing you know you got a jam session going right in the lobby without the piano or anything, just everybody would start playing and --
What did the hotel people do?

Listen, everybody would expect it, I guess, in most places, you know, and then they used to play at a place in Cleveland called Val's and Audile. In the Alley. That's where Art Tatum used to go and play. And he -- when he got off from work in Cleveland -- in fact, I think Art was working there.
And we used to all congregate at Val's In the Alley and play with Art all night, you know.
Val's In The Alley?

Val's in the Alley. And we would go -- then in Toledo he played at a place called Noble's, and we used to go down there, and that's wasn't Toledo, and we used to go down to Noble's and jam with Art. Everywhere Art Tatum was you'd find a session, you know, and you got a piano session or a few horns and (inaudible) because everywhere -- every city in the United States where Art had, where he played, he always had a place afterwards, some bar or some joint wher e he rented a piano, or if they didn't have one, kept tune and kept the icebox full of Pabst Blue Ribbon Beer --
Uh-huh, he liked those beers, didn't he?
-- and he'd go there and stay until daybreak because he never went to bed until daybreak. And he'd go there and all -- and all of the piano players of that area would collect there.

You know, it's been said that, you know, after Hawk heard Louis Armstrong, you know, when Louis came in Fletcher's band, that that turned him around. And also I've read that listening to Art Tatum influenced him, and I guess Art Tatum influenced all instrumentalists.
Art Tatum influenced everybody, but

one of the things, if you listen to Fletcher's records, and the big things that influenced Hawk all of them was Benny Carter. See, before Benny Carter came with Fletcher Henderson, Hawk was a rough tenor player. He played -- his style that he played, though, was very, very rough.
And after Benny Carter his style smoothened out, you know, became more fluid, because Benny had that influence, that smooth style playing.
You were telling me before when we weren't on taping that Don Byas used to play along with Tatum. Records
Yes, he bought all -- Ben Webster bought all of Tatum's records.
Uh-huh.
And Don Byas bought everything that Tatum recorded. I have quite a collection of Tatum too, but Don actually used to sit down and copy Tatum's solos and play them on the saxophone.

And he said that that's where he got his greatest harmonic education, by listening to Tatum. I'll tell you a story about Tatum. One time in Toledo when we had this gang. Well, Tatum had started making a little money, and he bought him a new Ford. And so he had a chauffeur, you know, and everything.
So we was up to one of the after hour spots one night and drinking a little of this lightning. And looked
around, and Art was missing. Now, where's Art, you know. So finally we went down, and he had gone down and gotten to the Ford and drove it right straight into a lamppost.
(Laughter.)
And he was sitting up there right in the Ford. He couldn't get out of it, you know.

So we got him out. He was juiced, you know. Finally we got him out of the car, and he had the car towed away and had to have it fixed. But he was like that, you know. He was very independent. He didn't like for anybody to help him across the street or anything. He played good pool, played pool, played penuchle, because he could see close, you know, if he had something.

You know, we had a band one time through the -- and I think -- I don't know what years it was, but it was in the '40s or '50s or something like that, and it was Max Kaminsky's band, Dixieland band. And they had Dick Carey on piano.
Did he double on peck horn?

He doubled on anything he could get his hands on, you know. We'd go into a place, and they had some instruments laying around. He just picked up -- it used to make Max mad, you know, because he would pick up anything and play on it, but it was Dick Carey and Al Hall and Jimmy Crawford, Ray Deal and Max and myself.

And so we were going to take a trip down in Virginia, but we had to stop off in Harrisburg -- I think that's Pennsylvania -- to play a night. So we played in Harrisburg. And so Max says, well, look, we'll hit on the road, and we'll go on down in Virginia, stop off at a motel on our way down, you know, before we get to this town in Virginia we're going to play.

So we left out from Harrisburg, and we would -- he had -- at this time Keg Purnell was playing drums, had three blacks, three whites in the band. So we stopped at this hotel, and Max would get out. So he used to come, said, 'Okay, fellows. The room's -- we can go in here. We can go in there
the guy would and see we're black guys, and they'd make some excuse that we couldn't stay there, you know.
Who would?
The manager of the motel.
You mean Max wouldn't tell them in front.

No, he just walked in and say, you know, and so that -- but then he got wind of this, and he -- and he started telling them in front, and then they started -- so we was going all the way down through to Virginia and couldn't get a place, couldn't get a motel.

So finally I said to Max, I said, 'Look, Max, let's go on into the town, and you take us to a certain -- to the railroad tracks, and I'll find a place. So we went into this town. I forget which town it was. It's down at one of the colleges, you know.
And we got to town and found the tracks, so I said, 'Now, just leave us, leave me out here and I'll get you a place to stay, and tell us where you're going to be, and I'll call you.'

So they went on to where the hotel where they were going to stay, because they couldn't get a hotel there, and we -- I found a rooming house. And we went on to the -- me and Keg Cake, me and Keg Cake --
And Al --

-- and Al went to the rooming house. And when they came -- I called them, and when they came to pick us up, we were sitting down eating fried chicken, and they said, 'Well, why didn't you bring us here to this place?' And we were having a ball, you know.

So we finally went on to this college to play this -- play this concert or dance. I think It was a dance. And there was a lot of Northern kids at this college from New York and everything. So the thing went over good. So they invited us to the frat house after we got through.

So finally Max said, 'You want to go?' 'Yeah, we'll go.' So after the job was through we went to this fraternity house, and these kids were having a ball. And so it was -- it was -- I've been (inaudible), and we're down here, and these girls and things were pulling on us and everything. I said, Max, I said, look. Let's get out of here, because first thing you know, if the cops come up here and catch us in here, we're all going to get a beating, you know.

Max says, 'okay, let's go.' So we left them. And just as we pulled out, the state troopers pulled in. Now, we're hungry. We're looking for a place to eat. Every place we stop, we couldn't get no place to eat. We're down below Washington. So just out of Washington coming up we find a Howard Johnson's, and so Max says, 'Let's go in here and eat. You know, we'll get something to see if the man will feed us.'

So Max gets out, goes into the cafe, and he asked, find out if they'll feed us. So the man said, 'well, we'll set you over in the back and the side, see. So he comes out, tells us that we could all go in to sit down and wait there until some of the customers start to get up and leave and everything.
And so the man finally decides that he wouldn't serve us.
Because he was losing all his --

Max jumps up on the stool and says, "Four score and seven years ago our ..." He started reciting the Lincoln Gettysburg Address, you know. And so I said, Max, you better come on. And the cook, the black cook in the kitchen was frantic. He didn't know what the -- he was back there looking, and he was afraid, see, because he said -- Probably these guys are going to get us all lynched down here.
And finally I pulled Max off the stool and we got back in the car and pulled off on away from there.
(Laughter.)
Yes, every time I see him, I start to --
Recite the Gettysburg Address?
Yes.
But, you know, obviously in traveling around all those years in, you know, with the bands you ran into this all the time.
Oh, well, you know, I know what to

expect because in the year earlier we had eaten in a -- many a kitchen, back up in a restaurant and also taken food out, and in fact, one time we was coming with Bernie Young's band and had gone down to Tulsa, Oklahoma. We -- some of the guys came back in cars, and Mike McKendrick -- I don't know if you remember him, the banjo player, used to be with Louis -- he and I came back on the bus, on the Greyhound bus.

And we were having a ball on the bus. I had my horn, and I'm playing, and Mike, he had his banjo, and the people were singing and everything. So finally we pulled into Kankokee, Illinois, to the bus stop for lunch or something. So everybody gets out and goes in to eat. Mike and I get on out and go in and sit down, sat there for about ten, 15 minutes, and nobody waited on us.
So finally the waitress came over and said, 'we can't serve colored people in here,' you know.
This was Illinois?
Yeah. So I said -- well, this is 1930, you see -- so I said, 'well, can we get some sandwich or something to go out?' And she says, 'okay, we'll fix you something to go out.'

Well, in the meantime Mike got mad. He goes out, and he -- he had a, was carrying a .45 pistol on him, you know, and he went out to get a policeman to find out whether we could. Anyway, while he was gone, the cook came running out of the
kitchen with a cleaver.
This is a white cook?
Yeah, he comes running out of the kitchen with a cleaver.
At you?

And -- but the waitress stopped him, you know, he come out, says, 'Didn't you tell those black so and so's that they couldn't eat in here?' And she says, 'well, they are going to take it out.' Well, I just got up. I was getting ready to let them have the stool.

And then when Mike got back, she had calmed him, and he went back in the kitchen. So I said -- I told Mike, let's go. We didn't even wait for the sandwiches, just went on out and got in the car. But he was going to --
If Mike had been there when --
If Mike had been there, Mike would have shot him, and we would have both been at Joliet, some place up there.
(Laughter.)
No, you ran into a lot of things on the road.
I remember in another town in Illinois with the Virginia Ravens we couldn't -- we couldn't eat there, or we couldn't sleep there, but we could play the dance.
We'd get in there, say, like at 8:00 and play the dance, start the dance at 8:30, and soon as it was over, we'd
leave and go somewhere else. Illinois was pretty rough in those days. In fact, The Loop in Chicago was bad news for -- you couldn't even go downtown and eat.
Well, New York was too.
Yeah, probably.

From what I hear. Not until, you know, the late '30s and before the war -- that it started changing somewhat. You know, even then you'd go down 52nd Street, you know. You could play, but you don't mix with the people or --

Well, in fact, in Florida you couldn't even play for a white dance in Florida. I remember when I was there with Ella, when I went to Florida, Chauncey Horton drew $50.00, he sent home and went down to the telegraph station. I get a call to come down there and rescue him because he had too much money. And they wanted to know where this guy got $50.00 at.

And I had to go and get him. He had sent money home to his wife, you know. And it was rough. In fact, they beat Buddy Rich up down there for trying to come and hear -- trying to hear Lucky Millinder's band. Lucky played there in the colored section.
Who was Buddy Rich with at the time?
I don't -- maybe the Tommy -- maybe the Dorsey Brothers, Tommy Dorsey probably.
And the police beat him up, huh?

Yeah. You remember the story of the Whispering Band of Gold? Well, that was a band out of Chicago. They went to Florida. This was in the '20s. And they -- some rich man hired them to play for a party, and some of the guys, the cops caught them and beat them up and beat the guy up that was giving the party.
And some of the guys were crippled for the rest of their life and some of them died from it, and broke up all their instruments. And it was quite a story.
The Whispering Band of Gold. Never heard of them.
Uh-huh.
Of course, the -- you know, as you were saying before on the -- when we were taping -- the smartest thing was the pullman in your own cars and the --
If you could -- well, Cab could afford that. Yeah, Cab and Duke could afford that.
But otherwise it was -- the musicians didn't want to go down South.

Well, I went down there with Benny Moten's band. We traveled all through -- in fact, that was our stomping ground, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas, Little Rock, Arkansas, and I went down there with Fletcher, and, well, you know, you just know where to go and where to stay.

I remember one time Benny Moten's band played at Beaumont, Texas, and Jimmy Rushing was sitting on the bandstand with white socks on, and a guy walked up there and pulled out his gun and said, 'Nigger, take those white socks off.'
(Laughter.)

I mean, so this kind of thing must have -- well, actually must have inspired feelings of frustration and hatred and all that, but it must have also, you know, you must have looked at those people and said how silly --
Well, some of them -- well, some of them were funny.
-- plain silly.
Some of it was funny. I mean --
Stupid.
-- some of it was very funny, and plus, it always happened -- I remember when I was living in Chattanooga --
Uh-huh, when you were sick that time.

Yeah. If you were -- you couldn't walk the streets at night if you were black, but I happened to know the cop on the beat, an Irish cop, and I could walk all through, used to walk, hey, Eddie, how you doing, everything,
